But even if my brain transposed the Virgin Mary into the dream because I was raised Catholic and the profundity of this peaceful feeling could only be understood or represented with something divine, where did that feeling come from? And why was it a one-time occurrence? I have no answers, so as a person of faith I've decided to take the blessing at face value and declare that if this wasn't a spiritual/religious experience, I'm not sure what is.

column37:
I haven't changed my vote in the sense that I voted differently before - I started reading SSC around 2015, when I was still in high school. As something I would consider a formative experience, however, it has significantly influenced my political outlook today. I used to hang out with the alt-right crowd, mostly out of a misguided sympathy with their plight for free speech. I still agree with them, somewhat. I never really abandoned the core values I learned as a conservative - I've just changed my perspective on them. Concerns about government inadequacy when it comes to taxes shifted from welfare programs to military spending; concerns about small businesses and competition were abandoned when I realized the republicans did more to support big business than anyone else; concerns about free speech were ameliorated when I realized most of the internet was less totalitarian than I thought. None of that could have happened without embracing the infuriating political middle ground your blog endorses.

Part of the reason I went into software engineering is because I started reading Less Wrong when I was 14. I knew, from prior experience, that I didn't have the willpower or interest to study computers in the context of a hobby. So I decided to do this professionally as a way to keep up with what is going on in the field of AI. Not to mention, I have the brain for it, which is a rare trait these days.

Slate Star Codex helped make my career decision in a different way. After reading you complain about residency and the FDA and Cost Disease, I pretty much ruled out medicine as a career choice entirely. I was already leaning "no" from my mother's experience as a nurse, but this sealed the deal.

column165:
For calibration, I was generally a very happy person growing up, and am still generally a happy person. I've also read and enjoyed a lot of very melancholy literature and been through phases of melancholy myself. I've also experienced some great successes, in sports when I was younger, and in various other things as I've gotten older. This is all to say that my "spiritual" experience was different from happiness or pride or satisfaction, all of which I'm familiar with. 

I've had a very few times in my life where I've felt something that is probably best described by "profundity." It's a feeling that some aspect of something is deeply right, like seeing my children happily playing together, though it doesn't happen anywhere close to every time I see my children happily playing together. In fact, it's only happened a few times in my life. But the feeling is so strong that it makes me think that it could be the basis for a religion, like if I were living thousands of years ago, I might have that feeling and think "That's it, that's what it's all about." But since I live now and I'm super not religious, I just take it as a sign that my lizard brain is pleased.

column165:
First an important note: I have mild bipolar I, diagnosed by a psychiatrist, under low-dose medication, extremely stable (no manic-depressive episodes in the last 4 years, and only 5 episodes in total since onset, with the first 4 being in the first year). Never done any drugs other than alcohol and caffeine, and I consume even these two in extremely low quantities (one glass of alcohol per year, 2 liters of coffee or soda per year). 

"Spiritual": I can essentially feel a strong emotional connectedness with the universe at will, though I ascribe it to a) reading the likes of Alan Watts and Raymond Smullyan (ALL their books) as an impressionable teenager, and b) after-effects of my bipolar disorder onset. I'm not in that state most of the time, and I don't think of it as paranormal ("real"), but psycho-biological. 

"Religious": I once had an argument with Yahweh about other gods in a dream. He wanted me to rejoin Christianity; I insisted there was no point in doing so when so many other gods are probably as real as him (i.e. probably not that real either); he finished the argument telling me to get closer to the other gods if that's what I really wanted to do. I don't believe in gods (individuals with a definite personality), nor that the dream was "real". (I believe in vague, unnamed, lowly-powered spirits or consciousnesses that go through the universe and merge or unmerge with each other...)

column165:
After taking a large quantity of psilocybin mushrooms and red wine, I had an experience of being able to observe how the mind creates a unified representation of the world in our subjective experience. It was rather liking being backstage at a play or seeing how a computer generated animation was made.
During a period personal anguish, I had a dream that I was in the crypt of the National Cathedral in DC. Guanyin, a Chinese bodhisattva, appeared to me and sang to me in Chinese as organ music resounded in the cathedral nave above. I was immediately comforted, and remained comforted after I awoke. I remembered the dream very vividly, which is uncommon for me. After waking up, I recognized the organ as playing the tune to 'Jerusalem' but don't know what the Chinese song was (it did not follow the melody, but was in a sort of counterpoint to the organ). I was raised Episcopalian and have spent the night in the National Cathedral before, and my mother wrote her thesis on Guanyin although I've only discussed it with her in passing.
I once saw a very beautiful statue of Apollo in a museum and it had a strange effect on me. After I saw it made me see much of my and other people's preoccupations as small and vain and caught up in illusion and self-deceit, and made me realize that the excuses I made for myself were lies. A year later I read a poem by Rilke ("Archaic Torso of Apollo") that indicated he may have had a similar experience, but I wonder if reading affects how I recall my own experience now. I don't think so, because I don't really like Rilke, and I distinctly remember being struck by the similarity at the time.

column37:
Mental illness related: My original solution has been to dissociate the 'affected' parts of my mind away from influencing any real-world behaviour. SSC (and the non-SSC LW Sequences) did help me in improving my explicit self-modeling and being able to constructively nudge/push the 'affected parts' into a healthy direction, which allows me to slowly refrain from dissociating the parts into oblivion.
Career related: I am starting my PhD and because of EA arguments, I searched for a topic that might positively affect my future impact instead of sth of pure academic interest (which had been my initial goal). Also, during/after the PhD I plan on properly assessing my future possibilities and choosing more carefully. SSC has been a constant source of 'this is how clear thinking looks like' and strongly helps with my motivation to improve myself.

I had a number of dejà-vu experiences (every severel months for the last few years), where I dream of a situation (mostly visual and the language-part of my thoughts) that feels somewhat weird (see example) and weeks/months later, I suddenly am in this situation and it now does make sense (and I remember my previous memory and confusion).
Example: I dreamt that I prepared a meal and as a finishing touch added milk. Then I ate the first bite and there was my thought "are you kidding me?". I was confused by this dream and didn't remember it until a few weeks later, where it actually happened (only this time I had the crucial information that I realised that the milk was spoiled and I had just ruined my lunch). 
I am unsure what to make of these experiences (in total, there were around 5 which seemed as if I should take them seriously) but as a physicist I updated towards increased credence for determinism (which seems important for 'remembering' the future).
column165:

My hypothesis is, that both feelings are created by the same part of my mind and both being somewhat exclusive towards each other.

I regularly experience "an extreme sense of connectedness, profundity, or presence", at seemingly random times. I feel emotionally overwhelmed, along with a deep certainty that the experience must *mean* something. It's often connected with a sense of being unmoored in time, with intense, multi-sensory flashbacks to seemingly innocuous moments in my past. It's generally prompted by intense or beautiful visual experiences, generally outdoors: a magnificent sunset, a view of the milky-way, mountains, the sort of "terror of the sublime" stuff philosophers talk about.

I'm a pretty stereotypical grumpy atheist skeptic, but I can 100% sympathize with the urge to label these experiences supernatural. I know they're *not*, that it's just a quirk in my software, so to speak, but my software's sending really loud messages to the contrary. Sometimes I'll have this... almost like an intrusive thought, just blaring in my head, "this is GOD. This is what people mean when they talk about GOD." Then it fades and I shake it off.

...I sound like the bad guy from some hokey Christian propaganda film, don't I?

column165:
Regarding energy work, when my father was ill with terminal cancer, his hospice nurse practiced reiki on him. It occurred to me that traditional medicine had literally nothing to offer him--there was no meaningful treatment for his cancer and chemo could only have extended his life for a few painful months. But he found the reiki very calming and effective. So, whatever it's purely scientific merits, it was a form of treatment that worked in that context. I found that interesting. 

Regarding the spiritual experience, I have had several deeply affecting dreams, some becoming waking dreams. The contexts differed (sometimes normal vivid dreams, sometimes associated with recent extreme experiences, or with sleeping partners), but in all cases my overall state of mind and personality felt altered for an extended period afterward (weeks). 

I also have had feelings of great connectedness due to (usually unexpected) extraordinary natural beauty (certain storms, certain secluded river valleys, certain ruins and abandoned structures, certain clear nights). I would say I have such experiences semi-regularly, especially when I travel. These are among my strongest and most pleasing memories.

column158:
I've had about six very vivid "waking dreams" that someone else might consider contact with supernatural entities, but they very clearly follow the patterns of sleep paralysis.  I was going to answer "no" above because they have a well-established non-supernatural explanation, but if I didn't know about sleep paralysis it would have at least seemed weird.

Example: In one I woke up while lying on my back, unable to move or breathe deeply, with a tight feeling in my chest.  I could see my room, and there was a shadowy figure hovering over me.  I could feel a strong presence from it that gave me a sense of its identity and state of mind (male, unfriendly but non-hostile, observing me but not intending to interact, etc.).  After about a minute, I snapped out of it and woke up properly.  Sometimes there's auditory hallucinations as well, like menacing laughter, or a hissing buzz that sounds like a paper towel slowly being ripped in half.  Sometimes these waking dreams are terrifying, but usually I just feel vaguely annoyed that the entity is paralyzing me instead of letting me interact with it.  It's always a different entity.  Usually when I wake up, it feels the same as waking up from a normal dream: It feels real while dreaming, but doesn't feel real after waking up.

column165:
I once had a dream in which a benevolent demonic entity/deity gifted me with a deep understanding of his most famous name (presumably to use as a component in spell-work or worship).  Because it was in his native language, the name was constructed of concepts and phonemes incomprehensible to a human mind.  But because I was dreaming, I could almost grasp it.  I woke up very slowly, which gave me a slow enough transition from dream-logic to real-logic to try to translate it into English phonemes and something my waking mind could grasp.  By the time I was fully awake, the name felt really mangled, but it was the purest form I could conceivably hold in my mind.  The plot of the dream made it clear that he had made a point to seek me out personally, he knew me fairly well, and he was taking a deliberate action to directly impact my understanding of him so that I could engage in spiritual/religious practices centering around him.

It didn't actually feel any different from a normal dream, so I assume that's what it was.  My dreams are usually very vivid, strange, and have a sense of "understanding beyond comprehension" or include senses I don't have in real life (like proprioception for all objects around me, based on their mass).  I also frequently have epiphanies in dreams that I "translate" as I wake up, usually to discover they're useless or don't make sense.  So the dream wasn't at all unusual, and I debated if I should even include it in the survey, but it seemed thematically relevant and I figured my answer could be tossed out if it didn't fit.

column165: I was driving late at night across a road constructed over a ravine. Just beyond the end of the ravine, I caught a deer in the headlights. I had an immediate vision of white light obscuring my view and an intense urge to get off the road (there was no shoulder, just a sheer drop into the ravine). I felt like the deer and I were somehow linked in this experience and as it was trying to run into the woods at the side of the road I had the fight to keep on the road or else I would go down the ravine, thus keeping the deer where it was. It was very difficult to keep my arms straight and keep the car under control against the urge to pull sharply to the right. All of the sensory data from my eyes was still coming through, but in my mind's eye the blinding white light was overlaying what I was seeing, obscuring my perception, even though I was 'seeing' everything normally. After a moment or two, I felt confident enough in my control over my arms that I could concentrate a little less on them and started slowing down, then I went over a bit of a up-slope in the road and the angle of the headlights changed to go over the deer's head, and the spell was broken. The deer ran off the road (to the right). I was free of the light and the urge to pull off the road. This occurred was when I was in high school, so I had hardly consumed any alcohol (certainly not on this night) and had not yet tried any other mind altering substances (not until I was 30). I've never had another experience like it.

column165:
Regarding the "Spiritual" category, on a nice summer's day I started a bike ride in the woods and began praying. I was thanking God for everything I saw (trees, birds, etc). Then as I continued to pray I began to thank Him for sight at all, and for hearing, and touch. Then I realized that beauty itself was a gift, and a started to thank Him that I could experience some things as beautiful, whether in sight or sound. I continued to thank Him in this was for some time, working my way naturally down to deeper and deeper levels. As I did I felt more and more profoundly connected to the world in a way I never had before, and never since. I got off my bike and practically kissed the ground: the world was so beautiful, and good, and was such a gift. I picked up a rock and stared at it: it was so beautiful. Everything was beautiful. Everything was a gift. 

I was not on drugs. The feeling could not last forever, but I will never forget it. 

Similarly many years later on a walk home after talking for hours with my wife to be, I truly connected with the realization that everything I worry about is less real than a shadow, and everything truly real was glorious and eternal. It is hardto describe. 

Regarding the "Religious" category I have had dreams that I have reason to believe may have given me insight into spiritual matters: specifically a glimpse of the divine nature (terrible to behold) and a glimpse into Hell. However they were dreams so they might have just been normal dreams. However I had each dream multiple times a year over the course of several years, and they felt different than my other dreams. But with dreams, who can tell? Perhaps they were just my way of mentally parsing my own conceptions of God and Hell. 

In brief the dreams were as follows:

I am standing in a field, and there is a forest in front of my as far as I can see to either side. The forest is old and dark, full of brambles, dead branches, spiderwebs, crawling insects, thistles, dead leaves, and all matter of tangled detritus one finds in old forests. I know that I must go through the forest to reach my goal, but I must not get dirty, or allow my clothes to be torn or disheveled. This is impossible: every time I go through I end up with torn clothes covered in burrs, webs, and pine needles. Sometimes in the dream I would encounter an ugly and mocking dwarf in the woods: sometimes a beautiful woman. In any case I would eventually break free and enter a clearing full of bright sunshine. At the center stood a pillar of water, and as I approached I was filled with a powerful sensation of the numinous. God was in the pillar, and his presence was awesome in the traditional definition of the world, and I was filled with holy terror. I knew that He was about to pass judgement, and I could hardly stand to be in His presence. I would always hear the judgement and awake, but I could never understand what He had said.  

In the second reoccurring dream I would be standing on a sidewalk: as far as I can see around me is manicured lawns, with a clean asphalt road next to me. Everything is peaceful and calming and I am terrified because I know what will come next. I am suddenly transported to The Machine. The Machine stretches as far as I can see in any direction: it is made of pipes and boilers and panels and bolts and general industrial equipment. The Machine is infinite. It is dark, and hot, and smoking inside The Machine and there is an overwhelming sense of doom and hopelessness. The worst is the noise. The Machine is a cacophony of gears turning endlessly, and of pounding metal. It is the worst sensation I have ever experienced.

I've had dreams, in the first-person, about boring or mundane situations (sitting in class, working at a desk, etc.), that have wound up happening exactly as they did in the dream, down to specific (non-boilerplate) exchanges, or myself trying to figure out why the situation seems familiar. I remember my dreams very infrequently, but these kind account for a significant fraction of those I do, maybe a quarter? Say, 10 times in all if I had to put a number to it, with a frequency of about once every few years (though I might have several in a row, or none for years). I've never been able to change anything I remembered, including my own behavior, though they're usually quite short experiences and by the time I've realized what's happening I'm already most of the way through it. 

I have also had your standard acid trip dreams where the floor is made of pasta or whatever, and also dreams about mundane situations that to my knowledge were just dreams (these are the most common among dreams I remember). I'm Christian, so I'm open to the possibility of the supernatural, but this also seems to be a pretty inconsequential waste of God's unfathomable cosmic power; mysterious ways, indeed. Let's just say I don't have a proposed mechanism.

A view behind the curtain, to the hidden machinery and motion all around. And joy. Joy that we can exist in a particular spot, in a particular moment, able to stand witness to something so far beyond our normal bounds of time and reality. column165: Regarding "Energy Work 2" -- Roughly once a decade I will have an experience while sleeping of extreme euphoria with a sense of being bathed in white light.  I've assumed it's some nocturnal release of a whole lot of endorphins or other neurotransmitters or something.  I've never had it while awake, but I imagine some ecstatic experiences derived from the "energy" traditions might feel the same.  Regarding "spiritual" and "religious" -- once after a very traumatic incident (suicide of a close friend that I had to tend to as the one-time EMT that I am and moreover had to inform his parents, talk to police, etc), I subsequently found myself walking outside in a city during evening rush hour and I suddenly had a several minute experience of feeling myself as part of a coherent meaningful whole with the many hundreds of pedestrians and cars whisking by me being not exactly the individuals I normally consider them... though not full ego dissolution and feeling we're all truly one... but we definitely felt nontrivially connected and, moreover, it felt "right" and "understandable"... like there was a purpose, ineffable but definitely positive and real, to all of existence.   This noetic revelation of a positive purpose to it all --- and not merely a sort of connectivity between all beings and events --- is why I answered not only I had a "spiritual" experience but an "unclear experience that seems it might belong in the ['religious'] category"

column158:
A few minor things, just enough for it to be noticeable. Like, sitting in one spot and then finding myself in another, a few meters away. The second spot is relatively untrivial to get into (it involved getting over our tent and a bunch of undergrowth), so I don't think I could (or had any reason to) easily wander there without remembering it.
Also, in some cases world appeared really really weird, like it was some usually ignored way of looking on the universe. That could be garden variety jamais vu, but I haven't felt that way anywhere outside our mystical practices. Ditto for some unexplained anxiety about *something being really wrong somewhere*. I'm not a very anxious person normally, and definitely not about some unclear wrongness in some distant location of emotional importance.

column165:
After a period of two or three days of isolating myself in my room, where I did nothing but sleep, I woke up and felt a great sadness for about an hour or so. Then there was a comforting, warm presence from inside me, followed by a strong urge to walk outside, for a very long time.

 I felt guided to walk outside by this presence, and went through places I'd been before and places I hadn't been before. I paused to look at buildings, trees, cars, birds and other animals. It seemed to me that I was perceiving objects at their true scale, which was much larger than they had seemed before. I also felt a bit disembodied; as if my sight was now slightly "zoomed in" and further away from me. Leaves in the wind and flocks of birds were suddenly much more beautiful and their motion was richer, more nuanced and more detailed. This made me cry tears of joy and feel very glad. I felt more aware of my smallness in the world.
After a while I no longer felt compelled to walk, bought two sandwiches at a bakery, ate them on the way back and went back to bed.

 As a consequence of this experience my mood improved a lot during the next few weeks and my mind felt much more clear. At the time I had decided that this meant I could die in peace and that it was no longer necessary for me to experience the world; I also instantly assumed, and frankly still believe, that experiencing this "comforting, warm presence" is what death feels like, and therefore i feel less afraid to die. I also feel my understanding of sound has changed as a consequence of this; I now appreciate a lot of normal everyday noises I didn't pay much attention to before and I enjoy some noises I used to find grating, overwhelming or otherwise distracting.

My religion teaches us to seek out spiritual experiences and so I recognize these quite often in my life. Most often, these things are what people might call 'feelings,' though I find the experience to be distinct from what people usually mean by the term. In our church, we are more likely to call them 'impressions.' These are usually small things, like a quiet, nagging feeling to give someone I haven't seen in ages a call or to talk to someone or go someplace without knowing why. Following those impressions sometimes takes courage and faith, but when I have done so, it has always turned out to be something good.

I have also been healed previously by the power of God and experienced things which I would say are direct communications from God, but these are difficult to describe to someone who does not have a shared religious vocabulary. 

I will just say that I have had enough spiritual experience to convince me that God is as real as anything else I experience.

column158:
Supernatural beings: I tried to run away from home on my bike when I was a teenager, but was stopped when a stranger on a tractor, who seemed to know what I was doing despite no outward signs that I was running away, told me it was getting dark and I should go home.  I started biking home, then looked over my shoulder to wave to the man, but he and the tractor had vanished.  I assume it was really just a perceptive local farmer, and he pulled into a hidden driveway or something, but it spooked me at the time.

ESP: When I was about ten, I went through a phase where I thought I could predict the outcomes of schoolyard basketball games.  I nailed my first few games, down to the exact score, and on one I predicted who would score the winning shot.  But after that I was right about as much as chance and I decided I had just gotten lucky.

I also sometimes have extremely vivid dreams that feel like I'm looking into a fully-formed alternate world.  These are the only dreams I consistently remember.

Other: I frequently experience deja vu and synchronicity.

column165:
When I was a teenager I went to a chiropractor for a pinched nerve in my shoulder. This chiropractor used a lot of what I now understand to be pseudoscientific methods and woo-woo stuff in her practice, though at the time I had no familiarity with those things and didn't really notice them - she didn't call them out or explain them. That day she did the back-cracking, light massage stuff she usually did, and then she sat me up and put a pair of big indigo-tinted glasses on my face. (She had a pair in every color of the rainbow on their own stand.) "To help with emotional release," or something like that. I was in pain and didn't much care - I figured after this I could just go home and lie down - but after a couple of seconds tears started running down my face. It didn't feel like an emotional experience - more a physical reaction. I remember turning to my mom, sobbing helplessly, and saying in a perfectly normal tone of voice through the sobs, "I don't understand why this is happening, wow, sorry." After a few minutes the crying subsided, and I went home. Pinched nerved resolved itself in a couple days, as they tend to do. 

I recognize now, after several years on the West Coast, that based on the color of the glasses and what she was using them for, she was probably trying to activate emotional release through unblocking my third-eye chakra. At the time I had no idea what a chakra was, and she explained nothing - "to help with emotional release" was the only explanation I got for what she was doing. I'm naturally very skeptical, and it's still the only time I've ever had a strong emotional reaction to someone trying to change my emotional state with spiritual work - since then at various times I've had massages from reiki practitioners, been on the receiving end of "energy work," and felt absolutely nothing. Never anything as immediate and physical as emotionlessly sobbing my eyes out. It was weird and out-of-character enough that it's stuck with me.

column158:
It sometimes feels like I can tell what's going to happen in the relatively near future even when I have no real basis on which to predict such things, in a way that feels similar to how one who is familiar with tropes can predict future plot developments in a book.

For example, if a female protagonist keeps having random positive thoughts about a male character, then immediately questions and dismisses those thoughts, you can be pretty certain that they'll be together by the end of the book/series.

Similarly, a few days ago I predicted (mostly in half-verbalised thoughts) that after three previous attempts, a certain phone call was going to go well, and that I was going to get an even better result than I should have.

If you read A Practical Guide to Evil, the feeling is sort of like how savvy characters can tell how a situation will go because of their familiarity with the workings of fate.

In reality, I'd put these feelings down to a combo of confirmation bias, unverbalised/gut intuition and hindsight bias.

column165:
I consider the specific “paranormal”/“mystical” distinction used in this survey to be very weird, and it carves a jagged blurry line through my experience set. Some representative examples of “magickal”/“theistic” experiences: I've had conversations with my patron deities and other etheric entities, and provided them with passthrough channels to use to have conversations with other corporeals. I perceive myself as having a natural magic field around me, and have manipulated it and/or made contact with other people's fields for various effects. I have had experiences of coincidences that strongly suggested interesting fate manipulation going on behind the scenes, including with “myself” among the sources (it's tricky to write about).

“Despite” this (though it doesn't *feel* contradictory to me), I hold a weakly-dominant hypothesis that these *could* be interesting emergent effects with poorly-understood/undiscovered physical representations—and I don't bind much to the term “supernatural”, because most people give that a certain elevated connotation, whereas to me these things are a natural part of my life which can vary widely in significance with the circumstances. None of my experiences have overtly contradicted macroscopic laws of physics, but some might require unconventional correlations to exist in the world for a physical interpretation to be compelling. This is e.g. why I answered “unclear” to “Spiritual” experience even though under *my* interpretation of the word I would consider the answer to be very much yes, because the question specifically calls out “completely distinct from ordinary life”.

column158: When I was a schoolboy, I spent the night at a friend's house, in a guestroom that contained several naughty Georgia O'Keefe prints. As I lay in bed, ready to drift off to sleep, I fantasized sexually about my friend's girlfriend. I woke in the middle of the night, and I had lost control of my body. I could not move my arms or legs, and my breathing assumed an unnatural rhythm (it came at greater and greater intervals, and each breath was sharper and shallower than normal: I cannot explain it well, I am afraid). My member became erect, but smaller than normal (I am not sure how I could tell this). I felt the sensation of a mouth on it, moving up and down, in fellatio. I was terrified. Since I was a faithful Catholic boy (with quite a lot of anxiety and depression) I imagined I was being accosted by a succubus. I repeated the name of Our Lord over and over again in my head (I could not speak). This finally seemed to break the hold on me. I leapt out of bed, flipped on the light, and prayed rosaries kneeling by the bedside until morning. Curiously, I believe that this was perhaps the last night that I fantasized about a woman for many years (I am homosexual). To be honest, I doubt completely that this event was at all paranormal, but I interpreted it as such at the time.

column158:
This would probably make me something of a pariah in LessWrong circles if I were open about it (...I hang out in rationalist-adjacent circles in Berkeley/Oakland/SF a fair bit), but I've had a number of experiences that I'd classify as "magical" or "paranormal," which I'm currently trying to make sense of, given my fairly decent knowledge of cognitive science, theology (broadly construed), and the philosophy of physics (...I'm not quite mathematically literate enough to "know" much about physics, aside from big-picture descriptions of how key theories work). These include what felt like contact with deceased people close to me, spells and invocations of deities (such as, say, Hermes, Hestia, and the Virgin Mary) having positive results, and astrology (the highly technical kind derived from Greek, Latin, and Arabic texts, not sun sign-related horoscope columns) "working." 

My best guess is that that part of it is confirmation bias and part of it is a consciousness-related mechanism similar to what Carl Jung calls "synchronicity." A probabilistic/physics-based explanation of this would most likely look something like Max Tegmark's "quantum suicide" thought experiment (in which one's subjective consciousness is effectively immortal because the Everett/many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics holds and whenever a random event happens that would cause one's death, "you" simply continue existing none the wiser in the universe where that doesn't happen). I know enough about philosophy of mind to be familiar with arguments for panpsychism and property dualism and take those views fairly seriously. I suspect that if they were true, we'd see similar types of phenomena, but would also not have to accept a more radical alteration of our current physical model than, say, the one implied by the transition from Newtonian mechanics to the standard model. 

As a sidenote, I'd highly suggest checking out this blog/nascent chaos magic community: https://runesoup.com. You and Gordon White (the author/moderator) have a fair bit in common re: interest in being data-driven and general distaste for online toxoplasma and I suspect that his writings and work by those he endorses might be a good "steelman" of pro-paranormal views, if you're looking for that. (I especially recommend this book: https://www.amazon.com/Chaos-Protocols-Techniques-Navigating-Economic/dp/0738744719 and would be curious as to what you'd think about this one: https://www.amazon.com/Real-Magic-Ancient-Science-Universe/dp/1524758825).

column165:
I have two separate things.

I have a physical therapist who has an unreal intuition for where tension in the body is and where it can diffuse to, who has literally made hip pain disappear by lightly touching muscles on my head. I was not a believer in any kind of healing touch, and I think most practitioners are total bunk, but I firmly believe that either she is the real deal or I have some kind of REALLY strong placebo effect with her, and not any other PT or massage therapist I have gone to.

Second thing. I'm not a professional meditator, but I do meditate sometimes and enjoy walking meditation. Twice in my life, I have experienced "trancendent" experiences where it seemed like time stopped, "no self", yadda yadda yadda. Once was when I was in a severe depressive state, the only one I had ever been in. It did not seem to immediately affect that state, but marked the end of an extreme apathy. The other time I was just out walking around by myself enjoying the nice summer day, and I looked closely at a black-eyed susan flower and disappeared into that no-self place again for what seemed like a very long time. This time I came out of that experience filled with a kind of weird lasting joy, laughing for no reason, etc... BOTH of these were before I ever experimented with psychedelic drugs, and were more powerful than anything I have experienced since.

If I had any religious bones left in my body after a terrible fundamentalist Christian upbringing, I would describe the second time as "seeing the face of god". As an atheist, I parse it as simply a strange hard-to-reach brain state that is incredibly uplifting.

column37:
Although I probably would have voted for Hillary anyway, SSC made me feel more confident about it, to the point that I tried to convince my family to do the same.  I now regret this, seeing Trump as a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to actually have a competent president.

SSC (particularly "NOBODY IS PERFECT, EVERYTHING IS COMMENSURABLE") helped me motivate myself to tithe to GiveDirectly for awhile.  I've since been convinced (by Tyler Cowen [Subborn Attachments] and others) that my own retirement account is the most cost-effective charity.

I probably eat slightly more meat because of SSC.  Scott is an example of a highly ethical person who eats some meat.  And his writings suggest that eating meat, while suboptimal, is no big deal, so that I feel less guilty when I deviate from my usual vegan diet.

column198: I have a much older half brother from my mom's first marriage, which ended quickly in divorce (soon after he was born). Then my parents met and had me. They then split up when I was 3 years old. They both eventually remarried. My stepfather's two sons eventually moved in with us (sequentially, not at the same time) and my stepmother's three daughters (from two previous relationships) moved in when she married my dad. My dad and stepmom eventually divorced after I graduated high school and then my dad married again to a woman who also had a daughter, who thus became my stepsister when we were both in college. I didn't include her in the survey because we were no longer living at home at the time. I like to say I'm an "only child of 7," though I do have a half-brother (11 years older than me). I grew up in Berkeley, CA, but I think this is atypical even for Berkeley. I feel I dealt pretty well with all of this change and in the end I think having all these people enter my life enriched it more than it detracted from it, and I'm glad my parents didn't stay together because they were terrible for each other though they both are/were totally lovely people in their own right. (My dad passed away a number of years ago.) I will say that all of this did make me very careful when choosing my spouse because I didn't want to repeat this pattern. As my mom likes to advise (referring to marriage), "If you can do it just once, it's better."

column165:
I must first remind you that I am a cold-hearted atheist of the Robert Sapolsky variety, but... 
When I was 13 I went on an evangelical-ish (think US bodies-hit-the-floor style, but in the UK) church trip. I had only attended for the social aspects and was invited by a friend, my family being irreligious. We had a total of nine sermons to sit through over the weekend. 

Anyway, during of them, I felt a wave of warmth - something like an adrenaline rush, but purely pleasant - course through my entire body. MDMA is the closest feeling I've had since, but this only lasted several seconds and felt... more real? (The only analogy I can think of is: if MDMA is McDonalds, this was Sunday dinner made by your mother.) As far as I can tell I did not move or give any signal of this to anyone else. About 1 second later, a nice woman named Anne, who was sitting behind me, put her hand on my shoulder and quietly said "I feel the holy spirit is upon you right now". "I know, I can feel it" I replied.

An that's when I became a born-again christian for two years. It didn't last too long because I was also very interested psychology and learned about all the ways people deceive themselves, also this was peak new-atheism time so I was familiar with (and eventually convinced by) all the usual pro-atheism arguments. Despite this, that moment still remains fairly inexplicable to me. There is, however, one way of reading it that maybe makes sense: 

In an alternative interpretation of events, what actually happened was that Anne put her hand on my shoulder first. Then I have something akin to an adrenaline rush due to surprise, but because I am calm and in a kinda spiritual mood, I find it a pleasant and warm feeling. These events happen so close together that they are put in the same frame of consciousness, so to speak; and because maybe I am on some level looking to be convinced, my brain represents the adrenaline rush as before the hand-on-shoulder to my consciousness. Alternatively again, during my christian phase I thought about this a lot and thus falsified my memory of the event to be more in line with my beliefs.

These interpretations do not convince me, however, because Anne was simply not the kind of person who would out-of-the-blue do that to someone. She didn't do or say anything like that to anyone else in the 3 years I knew her, she was quiet-ish and very normal. I think she really did sense something and I really did feel something unique and spontaneous, but I just can't explain it and don't believe in supernatural causes.

column173:
When anxious my visual-snow gets worse and I get after-images (neurological I think). I become more aware of floaters (detritus that floats inside the eye floating around).

Besides this I've got keratokonus, a problem with the shape of the cornea.
This causes "high order aberrations", like starbursts (crosses on top of lights), halos around lights and a slight duplication/double-vision when looking at high-constrast images (e.g. reading text in smartphone in a dark room). I become more aware of these when stressed.

I've asked an ex-girlfriend and my mother whether they can see visual-snow when looking at a white-wall in a dimly light room, they both did.

I think the phenomenon is common and usually benign. It gets worse/bothersome with anxiety.

Still strange how little is written about it.

Early in December I had a dream that the last official thing the leaving president did was to give Professor titles to 12 people, including the head of my department (because the new president wouldn't do that because he didn't like those people or some other silly reason). Energy Work 2 - I have had moments of connectedness with the past, if you've read Proust, it's a lot like that. An echo of a past moment from years ago that is closer to you than yesterday.  Spiritual/Religious -' I did 150ug of LSD after a 3-day fast which made me experience the world in a different way. I had an experience that could be comparable to "harmony of the spheres" in the astrological sense. A thing has certain modes of being that are according to the nature of things. It's difficult to translate the sense-experience into words. Very cliche, I know. I've also semi-successfully conducted magical rituals to reel in a binge eating disorder (undiagnosed, but I had several days where I ate 5000+ calories for 3-4 days). I acknowledge that magic isn't about throwing fireballs, but altering your state of mind. It's like a pep talk, except externalized and amplified. A prayer. A conjuring of a goal-oriented belief. 

Maybe it would be best to just throw out this section all together, since I don't think how we think about things like "believe", "real", "physical law" or "normal conception" match onto these things very well.

when I was little, I have to confess, I watched DBZ and- while not thinking any of it was real- I played with trying to feel some analogue to the 'chi' business. With some focus, there was a definite tangible sensation to it. Tiny-me thought of it more like a form of meditation and figured that feeling is probably the basis of chi-ish stuff.

Regarding the 'connectedness' one: in the worst part of my depression, I had trouble understanding people and was mostly irritated by them, sometimes moving towards a deadened, cold kind of hatred, intermingled with dread. When I started recovering, the first emotional capacity I got back was sadness. Extreme suffering/death in general was a pretty constant mental attractor. For about a year I cried myself to sleep almost every night to intrusive thoughts about everything terrible- not confined to myself. Sometimes this lead to a profound state, like a really warped metta meditation. It's hard to hate someone, even someone being an asshole, when it feels like watching a rescue of a malnourished dog hiding under a truck, scared out of its mind, biting at the person's hand because everything has been so horrible for so long.

column165: I've definitely had moments of feeling deep peace and connectedness, but (despite having one of them while visiting the Ba'hai Lotus Temple) I wouldn't describe it as 'spiritual'. I don't feel like my overwhelming positive feelings reflect real or numinous things outside of me any more than my overwhelming despair during depression reflects something real or universally fundamental. It's a mood that I occasionally have the fortune to enjoy, and usually connected with wonder at the natural world or human striving. The earliest incident I can remember I was taking a poetry class at summer camp, and we went out into the yard and I decided I was going to just try to *listen* to everything at once, because my dad had talked to me recently about trying to list to everyone in a crowd. And after a little while it was like a switch flipped, and I *could* hear everything at once - my classmates talking, and the wind in the trees, and the rumbling air conditioner next to the building and a half dozen other things. I felt like it was pouring into me or I was pouring out into all of it. I felt light and bright and wide open and joyous. It was such a mundane place and mundane moment but it was so beautiful. The clouds were beautiful and the grass was beautiful and the crouching square rattling bulk of the air condition was beautiful too. If there was a presence it was the presence of the whole *world*, that I normally bIocked out, and it was profound that I could experience a bigger wedge of it than usual, but that itself felt like profundity enough. I think it's wonderful that my brain has the ability to process stimulus like that, even if I can't predict or control it. I wrote a poem about it that wasn't terrible for a teenager. I don't pine for that moment but I'm grateful that I had it, and I'm confident I'll feel similar things every once in a while if I take my antidepressants and let myself be open to it.

column165:
I did a Buddhist pilgrimage in Japan in my early 30's. Among other things, I had a really irritating infection vanish shortly after I prayed about it. I also had very strong feelings about my physical safety, the presence of spirits, both benign and malevolent, and "help" navigating that I felt came from somewhere other than strictly inside of me. I was struggling between trying to open myself up spiritually and being really skeptical for the whole pilgrimage. For comparison, I tried pretty hard to become similarly inspired and spiritually engaged as a child going to Mass every day, but it was never like that. There was always an aspect of "fake it till you make it," with Catholicism that wasn't there during the pilgrimage. I was also getting massive amounts of fresh air and exercise, which may have been a factor. 
Also, while I don't do "energy work," I see a massage therapist regularly who does deep tissue massage, and it can get very emotional and trippy.

column158:
I am often able to accurately tell what people are thinking of.  For example, back in high school a girl I knew somewhat but not well suggested that her choice of car might be "a little weird"; I said "a Wrangler is not weird," and was right.  I suspect this is due to my memory, which has been described by others as weirdly good; I remember very old conversations down to the wording.  I would connect that idea with the fact that I have eclectic taste in movies, music, and other culture.  I tend to think of myself in relation to various fiction narratives; plausibly I would be able to put myself in someone else's shoes if I could get a few base details from them about how they think of themselves in the same terms, and use that to understand what they are thinking in the future.

Just a guess.  The only bits I am sure of are that my memory has been described by several people as unusually good, at least in regard to social interactions and culture, and that I've been able to predict what people are thinking often before they express it.

column158: I have been involved in occult communities ever since I was a young teenager. If you spend enough time in these sort of circles, paranormal experiences begin to see mundane and difficult to point out as notable from any other normal experience, so my answers reflect a broad range of events rather than single "ahah!" moments that most people have. Nevertheless I can point to several minor encounters with gods, mostly negative, never physically present but represented as out-of-context feelings when attempting to contact them. I was witness to a possession once, and either it happened or the woman was an extremely good actor. This event was also preceded by another person warning the woman of imminent danger, so either he sensed it or this was all planned as a trick for some reason. Beginning "psychics" or magic practitioners tend to practice with sensing games, or Remote Viewing games. I used to be quite good at them, but second guess myself too much now adays. I'm still quite good at predicting the future though, as far as psychics and magic users are concerned. I've been witness or the direct participant of many events that follow a "I'm going to do this" and then "something weird happened that is entirely in expectation of doing 'this'" happened, so many that it's difficult to count. One recent event of this type was I had a practising friend of mine take a look at my "fate path", for lack of a better term, because I felt something was wrong and upon having this done I felt significant physical pain and an inability to keep my eyes open or straight. This happened once with my expectation, and again an hour later, to which when I asked about it, it was exactly in time with my friend getting a second confirmation from one of her own friends. Beyond that if you want something more spectacular, I've heard second hand accounts of accidental stuff like teleporting small objects, or bringing a dying cat back to health, but these things are difficult, or impossible to recreate intentionally. I do have a friend who knows somebody who is able to consistently win at slot machines or other games of chance, due to magic. You might think this should be expected and common if magic was real, but this is quite difficult for normal magic practitioners, so knowing somebody who can do it consistently is noteworthy. Finally, I used to have out of body experiences quite frequently. These things are all just some of the more noteworthy things.

column158:
As a kid and teenager, I had experiences of "waking up" to see a ghost who I instinctively felt was my late grandfather sitting at the end of my bed, and of grey aliens being in my room.  I also had one experience of my brother (7 years old) and I (10 years old) being unable to sleep one night due to an eerie flute music coming from a home in our neighborhood under construction; my brother and I remember us keeping it awake, but my parents couldn't hear it. 

While I was convinced at the time that I was awake and having these experiences, I now firmly believe they were dreams and/or over-active imaginations.
column165:
Not sure if this is the correct category, but I was thoroughly indoctrinated into Christian Science, as a child.  It's a faith healing religion based on the premise that if God is good, then sin, sickness, disease and death LITERALLY do not - CAN NOT - exist.  If you are experiencing one of those things, then it is capital-E Error, and "praying" is basically pretzel-twisting your mind into denying reality until the unpleasant experience goes away.  

I believed all of this as a kid, but was gradually confronted with reality in young adulthood, and eventually wholly rejected it in favor of atheism.

column37:
Donating more (and more effectively) and eating less meat were both part of my Peter Singer-inspired initial discovery of EA. 

I was in touch with 80K hours and received coaching on a career in AI safety, but have moved away from that in light of, 1) Making it through to final rounds of Oxford fellowship and then being rejected, 2) Feeling like 80K did not have a great grasp of what a lawyer could even help with beyond a vague research/policy/prestige contribution, 3) Feeling like 80K did not understand what the important checkpoints/markers of a legal career were, to the point that their advice might really mess up my career capital/prospects, 4) Thinking, over time, that the AI risk concern itself was a bit less practically/morally important, 5) Just a general disillusionment with EA and 80K, feeling that EA was trending towards a self-consciously weird/contrarian image and 80K was trending towards a single focus on the long-term, yet channeling people into very conventional, high-prestige roles in, e.g., government to have an impact on the long-term. Overall, I have cooled off greatly on the idea that the EA community has a particularly good idea of what any particular person should be doing with their life. I do have an enduring interest in national security and emerging technologies from my dabbling with AI safety, but I expect to engage that from a much more traditional legal perspective rather than using every ounce of credentials I have to land a policy research job with OpenAI or something similar.

column165:
Spiritual' is ambient, more of a waxing and waning than discrete; the episodes can persist for days.  Strongest ever was prompted by a John Cage performance- extreme sense of awe about my experience of and participation within reality.  Wandered around campus just listening to ambient sounds and feeling amazing until my schedule demanded more practical activities.  "Jhana" might be the closest term?

the religious experiences are more acute but very brief- i.e. once I was praying as part of an experiment back when I argued about religion on the internet a lot, and it induced one.  The 'presence' of a divinity was extremely palpable as a feeling, and right at the climax of it a poster fell off my wall and freaked me right the heck out.

Most recent example: after wandering around the desert for several days as part of my job, just before sleeping I had an acute sense and visual hallucination of being tormented or attacked mentally by a demonic presence.  I texted my boyfriend (who is religious/catholic) to ask him to pray to make it go away, which worked, but it's the first time I got a visual aid for one of these things.

None of these have prompted religious conversion or affirmative beliefs, but they're not uncommon- months to years between episodes, persistently since youth.

column37:
Partly because I was inspired by some of the posts in this blog, and partly because I was inspired by someone who was inspired in turn by this blog, but I have taken initial steps to getting a therapist. These have largely been unsuccessful, mostly because I'm very bad at doing paperwork and/or talking on the phone, but I'm trying. (Unrelatedly, would you possibly consider giving that question above about whether we have attended SSC meetups an additional option: "No. I want to, but I'm bad at doing things.") 

I read a lot of posts in this blog over a few months (mostly because I'm in recovery from a reddit/quora/imgur/ao3 addiction, and this blog is something I actually feel like I can read in moderation), so I might have everything all jumbled up, but here are a few posts that really spoke to me:

I loved the thing you wrote about people who have low level paranoia, but not enough to be seriously obstructive to their life. The kind where someone you know is kinda rude once and suddenly you're like "wait, what did I do that that person suddenly hates me so much", but actually it's because their brain is just twisting this. I just had always assumed that everyone was like this and that the reason it's such a problem for me is just that everyone else was more rational than I was and that they are able to immediately logically convince themselves that it's not like that meanwhile I'm still trying to convince myself that it's okay hours later.

Also, I just generally liked all the posts about how we all have a bias towards believing that other people's brains are just like our brains. I didn't change my vote in any elections, but I will say that I had been one of those people who were like "pro-lifers obviously just hate women", but now I see where that reasoning went wrong.

(Also I reduced the amount of meat I eat over the past few months, but I'm not sure it's because of this blog; it's a confluence of many factors.)

I was a petty criminal/thug as a youth and associated with other petty criminals on a locally notorious council estate.

We were subjected to stop and searches frequently, sometimes, especially following a serious crime or an upwards trend in crime on the estate, these would result in heavy handed tactics by the police. One trick was to drag one of us into a riot van, give us a beating to the body, take our possessions (usually drugs and money) then drive us to the other side of town and throw us out of the van.

NB: the majority of encounters were not like this and I was one of the worst kids in the worst gang in a bad neighbourhood. I believe most police officers are good people.

It wasn't a waking dream - it lasted far too long (several minutes), and didn't vanish even when I reached out to touch her. I don't think I've ever written this down before, and feel very uncomfortable about it. I'm not communicating how RIGHT it felt. This was more than thirty years ago, and the memory still brings me peace.

A spiritual experience I have somewhat regularly is thoughts that appear (either in the moment or later) to be not my own. On a few occasions, these thoughts include creepily accurate premonitions of the future. I don't have any personal examples that make good stories.

I suspect my father has something similar, as evidenced by his ability to guess correct answers to questions. Two examples: In college, he passed a multiple choice test which was entirely in Korean (he speaks English and some Japanese). The best example I've seen is him correctly guessing which Alexandrian bishop did [something I forget] using a name he vaguely associated with Mardi Gras (he's never studied early church fathers) - note this was not a multiple choice question.

There are times when I feel more or less of God's love. My most vivid experiences with this are mostly from feeling an absence of God's love. I think this is uncommon in my tradition - I've told people that I have more clear negative spiritual experiences that positive ones.

Since my ability to feel God's love roughly corresponds to me choosing things in line with God's will, I've tried to make this into something to help me make hard decisions. Reduce the problem to sequence of binary decisions; for each decision, try each option and feel for the response. This process often doesn't work because the spiritual difference is subtle / unclear, but it has worked for some things, so I try it.

column158: I am prone to hypnogogia. Most of them are devoid of obvious meaning or intent. But now and then... there's a personality there. In one of these, a voice clearly spoke to me. It was overwhelmingly warm and gentle. It influenced my decision to marry my husband. No, I will not tell you what it said. Only that I felt heartbroken by its absence, once I was fully awake. I have had many classic sleep paralysis episodes, and nothing can convince me that there is NOT a malign supernatural entity involved in those. But I understand why many people write this off as a strictly psych/neuro phenomenon. In addition, I once dreamt I knew the password to the classroom computer, which nobody had told me. I tried it, naturally. It did not work. Eventually, when I was given the password, it turned out to be one digit off from the one I'd dreamt.  Coincidence? Did I overhear it on a subconscious level? No idea.  I would, however, like to point out that these experiences were all very different in quality from definitely-hallucinations I used to have, back when I suffered a hypothyroid episode, and was constantly seeing cats (dark movement) in my peripheral vision. They are also noticeably different from  my usual (abnormally high?) level of weird visual phenomena (phosphenes, visual snow, synaesthesia). I knew those were strictly neurological phenomena, even while they were happening.

column158:
Supernatural beings: When I was about 5 years old I thought I encountered a ghost. I don't think it was real now, and think it could be explained by me just experiencing a strong sensation of being watched.

ESP: I have had multiple dreams in my life that seemed to be mundane premonitions of future experiences. Examples include dreaming of my future wife 16 years before meeting her, conversations with future co-workers, situations in college, situations in public, etc. Individually they all seem to be explainable as a coincidence. But I have had more than ten of these dreams. I still put this in the 'sort of' category, because I didn't catalog any of these dreams. It could be an overactive sense of deja vu.

Spiritual: When I was in my teenage years I had a few times when a I felt a profound sense of understanding of the word. Like everything suddenly clicked and made sense. Certain drug experiences sound very similar to what I felt, but I was not on any drugs. However, I think I was probably masturbating for hours straight beforehand, so I might have somehow drugged myself on my body's own hormones. I was a pretty fucking horny teenager, so the hours straight of masturbating weren't out of the ordinary.

Spiritual: I also had a few instances of a profound emotional disconnect.  Almost out of body experience, like I was an observer of my body and all of its emotions, but that the body and those emotions were unattached to 'me' the observer. I was an asshole if I interacted with anyone else during this time period, because I wasn't really feeling any empathy. I think of them as psychopathic episodes. No idea why they happened.

column165:
I used to be regular about scripture study and prayer, and had a period from about 2001 to 2012 where I was able to internally "hear" answers to specific questions, including information about what would happen in the future. Sometimes answers were, "that's not for you to know." Often, answers were directive "go here, focus on this, this is where you should be." Yes or no questions were easier to discern.

When depression wasn't interfering with my ability to feel, I also felt tremendously loved when I received these answers, which was unusual compared to my upbringing. Even when I had difficulty with emotions, I could still listen. In retrospect, it has a lot of similarity to meditation, but it felt like communication with somebody else.

After military deployments, this became much more difficult.

There are times in which I believe I am directly experiencing the presence of God, not through obviously supernatural events like a burning bush or being "touched by an angel", but through feelings of hyperfocus, benevolence and love to all (especially those who wish me harm), and a profound sense of gratitude. It is as if for a moment I as a temporal creature am able to hold onto atemporal existence while connected to source of all existence. I can never sustain this experience for very long (sometimes moments, sometimes 2-3 minutes). Sadly, we beings who are slaves to time and space cannot transcend those boundaries, but I believe we can momentarily experience a foretaste of existence without them. 

This could be my own delusion, but even if so it inspires me to continue to become a better person and to manifest the will of God to as well of a degree as I can understand such an ineffable concept (which is to say, quite poorly).

column158:
After studying occultism for a few weeks as a young teenager I tried a ritual I found online. Nothing happened and I didn't feel anything. I went about the rest of my day and went to bed. After about an hour of not sleeping (normal for me) I saw a soft green light at the foot of my bed. It got brighter and slowly rose into my field of vision. The thing was a ball of light-green light, without well defined edges. It was brighter at the center and diffused out around its radius. The thing hovered a bit above my laying down eye-level for a few minutes, sorta pulsing it's brightness level. It was accompanied by a sort of feeling of a presence, like how it feels to think you're in the same room as someone else, or a dog or something.

Eventually the thing started pulsing slower and expanded to cover my entire bedroom in a very mild green light. The light cast a shadow on my wall of something that wasn't in the room. I want to say it was of an arm and hand, with the fingers spread as if to grasp something, though it happened so fast I couldn't really make it out. The shadow was really large, implying whatever cast it was either big or close to the light source. After I saw the shadow the light entirely dissipated and I went to sleep. 

Some time in the next few days I felt a weird sensation while I was by myself. It was like there was a very minor presence in the room with me. I had a weird thought like "Hey that green light thing's back and wants to talk". The voice in my head was my voice, but knowing myself I'm pretty sure I wouldn't think that. Like 90% sure. I thought to myself "Hey green light, if you're back make me feel" and then I said a word I use to myself to describe a very particular internal mental feeling. Immediately I felt it. I don't know if I was just hyping myself up to feel it. I guess that would be possible, it was all just feelings in my head. I asked the thing to make me feel two different feelings and both happened.

At this point I got nervous and realized there's no effective difference between talking to a weird spirit or demon or whatever that's real but only in my head and being crazy and thinking I'm talking to one. I tried to convince myself in the moment that I just hyped myself up into feeling positive responses I wanted and didn't address the light anymore. The vague feeling of presence went away and I never had an experience like that again.

A few years after this I started playing around with lucid dreaming and sleep paralysis. I would frequently run into this character, who would always look like some random person I know with distorted facial features. Even if he was in a female body, he would have a very rough masculine voice, like a chain smoker's. If I was in a regular dream, it would immediately become lucid if I ran into him. If I was in a lucid dream, I would run into him about half the time and then quickly wake up. He always seemed annoyed or pissed off at me, either for bothering him, not knowing something, or "not figuring this all out yet". A few times he would give me vague hints to "this all". One that I still remember was "I am part of you, but not entirely of you." Now that I type this out, I wonder if this dream character is related to the green light.

column165:
Energy seems obviously real to me, though I'm a bit confused about the "not while meditating" disclaimer, as meditating is a good way to get access to it, and meditation seems to change your brain in ways that persist off the cushion.

Through meditation and careful body awareness (which quickly developed into an "energy" ontology), I've developed partial control of things like level of inflammation in my sinuses, how energetic I feel in the morning, and whether my experiences cause positive or negative emotions. I also have a strong track record in being able to stop other people's hiccups with energy work, albeit with low N and very unscientific test conditions. It seems entirely possible to me that I'm at the very bottom of this skill tree.

None of this seems to require novel physics, just novel psychology.

column165:
I was 17. Summer holidays before upper sixth. Went for a walk near my house (in the country) down a lane. I was talking to myself (as I often do, just to help organise ideas, clear my head). on impulse, I sat on a gate (I remember this all very clearly, I could describe the gate, tell you which side it opened, which way I was facing, I remember taking off my hat and how I handled it, twisting it about as I sat etc.). I looked at a tree growing by the side of the path. I had an experience, probably lasting about 5 minutes (at this point I was no longer talking to myself) of understanding the tree and it's surrounding environment (including myself) at many different scales and many different terms.

To clarify: I 'saw' the way the tree could be broken down into different components and this even in different ways (one could divide by materials into bark, outer wood, heartwood, leaves etc., OR by environ into trunk, branches, sub branches, twigs etc.), then how each of these could be broken down in different ways again, and again into increasingly fundamental things. I don't know much natural science, but this part of the experience ended with understanding the fundamentality of some basic particle (I'm not going to say 'atoms' because even I know that atoms are by no means the most basic particles, and anyway I mean 'basic particle' in a more philosophical sense: a basic thing, substance or type of which there are may instances). Then the experience reversed, going 'out' rather than 'in', building back up to the tree as a single unitary whole, but then further, to include the tree (and it's parts, and all the different ways of seeing them) as components in increasingly large, complex composites: how the tree related to the other plants and animals around it biologically, how (with various different conceptions of 'physical') all objects were physically connected or related or distinct,  or indistinguishable. This continued to the whole of reality. it is important to stress that this did not include realisation of physical, scientific 9as in conceptual/categorical) and metaphysical relations, but also of relations like family (when the model became large enough to include me and other people, especially those I knew) and friends. 

And that's why I chose to study philosophy.

My parents split up when I was five months old. By the time I was 1, my father and mother had both moved away from the city I was born in, both remaining in the country, and my father was living with a woman who would be his long term partner (they are still together). I lived with my mother and had regular contact with my father (visiting for weekends every fortnight). When I was 5 a girl was born to my father and his partner. When I was 7 a boy was born to them. My mother remained single and did not have any more children until I was 19 (when she had a girl). 

In the above, I counted my stable immediate family home(s) as my 'household'. So my household contained two later social siblings and no further biological siblings (until I was 19, but the question asks until 7).

1. I drank two beers and I was at a punk concert (very loud, monotonous rhythmic music). I felt and "saw" myself became Yamantaka, a six-armed deity from Tibetan Buddhism. I felt powerful, capable, strong, fierce.
2. I was at a jazz concert (I don't like jazz, the music felt like white noise with no rhythm). I "saw" Amaterasu (Japanese goddess of the sun) descend from above, she hung in the air and extended her arms towards me. I was dealing at the time with transitioning (female to male) and I felt that Amaterasu accepted me for who I am. I started crying.

I have a vivid visual imagination and thus "seeing" things that are generated inside my head is not drastically different from seeing with my eyes. However, I did not consciously decide to "see" them at that time. Imagining them right now has no emotional impact on me.

I study Comparative Religions/Buddhist Studies. I do not "believe" that Yamantaka or Amaterasu are "real". I was an atheist before, during and after these experiences.

column165: Sometimes, usually after meditating (not so much during, which doesn't count anyways), everything will take on a sort of "raw" feel to it, like I'm not imposing my own interpretation onto sense data. Usually it's most profound with the visual sense. Like, I can still perceive and identify objects, but any narrative sense of what they are or how I relate to them is more or less gone. I can still recall what it would be, but that recall itself is just another object. So like, if I look at my hands I see hands, and can even identify them as my own hands, but they don't *feel* like my hands (even though I still have a sense of proprioception in them). This has made it abundantly clear to me that the seeming solidity of everything is just sort of something that gets added in when I'm not really paying much attention and has caused me to question pretty much all of my own phenomenal experiences and the assumptions I have about them as they relate to a sense of identity (in particular because if you pay close enough attention identity is just something in your field of senses and it shifts in clever and subtle ways all the time).

Friend came back with a gendarme, Duoanes took my friend in, told gendarme to leave. Searched our stuff, said they were looking for guns and drugs. We had nothing, but then said I could be charged with resisting arrest, but ultimately just let us go.

I also place more stock in the general concept of that type of premonition because my mom, a very down-to-Earth person, swears that before I was born and even before a doctor told her my sex, she KNEW I was going to be a girl with light hair and green eyes (notable because both my parents have dark hair and brown eyes).
