column165:
Energy work 2: Doesn't actually feel mystical to me, but my martial arts instructor showed me (and semi-scientifically described) techniques for internal alignment that improve your physical structure to a completely ridiculous degree. I'm talking like, making yourself significantly harder to move, or hitting harder, in a way that seems magical. We did one exercise where he instructed us to point a hand and imagine ourselves shooting a jet of water out of our fingertips toward the farthest point we could visualize. When I wasn't focused on the visual, anyone could easily yank my arm down, but when I was focused, my training partner (8 in taller and 50 lbs heavier than me) couldn't move my arm. And I'm not even any good at martial arts. My instructor can do stuff with his structure that looks like pure wizardry. So could someone use various practices you mention to improve their internal physical alignment, literally just aligning their own muscles better, even by accident, in a way that feels mystical? Sure, why not.   


Spiritual & Religious: I answered "yes" to both based on the same experience. My senior year of undergrad (the 2017-2018 academic year) was really rough in a lot of ways, especially academically--I was going through a crisis about whether I was capable enough to enter a graduate program in the physical sciences, mostly because I was failing my exams for reasons totally unclear to me. Exams made me panic horribly, to the point of self-harming. The second piece of the weirdness of senior year was a religious crisis; I'd found out one of my best friends, "John", was (still is) a Calvinist and our frequent debates made me confront my own beliefs and ethics much more intensely than ever before. Eschatology is the mind-killer. To be clear, I don't AGREE with this guy, but he had a serious philosophical structure and I was still working through mine. By the end of senior year, I was mentally exhausted and had given up on trying to settle philosophical/theological questions in my own head, and just was trying to pass my finals. I was agnostic (although I'd already ruled out the pantheons of neopaganism as a religious option, for unrelated reasons), and also quite an angry person--maybe God exists, maybe not, but either way I'm furious at him. What use is God, but a good place to direct the anger at the world's injustices that has no other outlet. But, occasionally, I would pray (yell?) to God that if he were real, he'd tell me so directly. My stipulations were: not while I'm drunk or extremely tired (so I'd know it wasn't an altered state of mind), not in a location you'd expect to have mystical experiences (not in gorgeous scenery or even preferably any religious building), and no ambiguous signals I was expected to interpret, nothing I had to pattern-match to understand. I told God, "If you're real, you know what would convince me even better than I know myself, and you know I have a stubborn, skeptical mind. It has to be personal, direct communication, something I can't deny." (Giving a hypothetical God a list of criteria for personal revelation is not quite the most Jewish thing I've ever done, but it's pretty up there.)    

The night before my last final, for my worst damn class, I was trying to study and kind of thinking in the back of my mind that it was just a matter of time before I wanted to self-harm that evening. I was in a clear mental state, wide awake and sober, and to work off some nervous energy, I went to pace in my favorite pacing spot--an extremely mundane blank hallway of the science building, not exactly where you'd expect any mystical experiences to strike you. As I walked, my legs suddenly felt extremely weak and began to buckle, so I sat down against the wall. As I did so, I felt as if I were completely surrounded by a single, invisible, conscious presence, which communicated to me an immense love and told me (not in words) that, as a person, I was inherently valuable. I wasn't hearing or seeing anything; the message wasn't an auditory hallucination--I just absolutely knew that Someone was with me and communicating these things. I can't describe how good it felt. My anger had been heard, and accepted for what it was, and not condemned. My fears about my future had been heard, and answered; nothing about my future was promised except that my worth would never lie in the things I was so worried about. The presence was so real that if I wanted to doubt it, I would also have to start doubting the material existence of everything I could see and touch. And all of the criteria in my sort-of prayers had been completely met. I stayed there for a couple of minutes, but finally I had to get back to studying. The purity, the intensity of the presence faded, but when I went back to my notes, I still felt clean and joyful and accepted. A little while later, John came by to check on me, because he knew about my previous self-harm and was worried about how I was doing before the exam. (Calvinists are mysterious. John demonstrates an enormous amount of compassion and tolerance, despite believing in and loving a wrathful, damning God.) If I had any doubts about how serious my experience was, they were dispelled when John (a normally very unobservant person) immediately told me with great surprise that I looked different--calmer, in much better shape than he'd expected I'd be.  

I failed the exam dramatically--my worst of college--and it was fine. I was so much more okay after it than after any other exam. I got into a graduate school that I really like. I'm doing research I love. That's not to say I don't still have doubts or old, bad habits. I've self-harmed since then. I still have a lot of anger and sometimes that still spills over into anger at God. I've struggled with the amount of stock I should put in the experience, but like I said--if I doubt that, I have to doubt everything. And I know some people really do live with doubt about the existence of everything, but I can't live like that. Still, believing that there is a good, non-material creator doesn't tell me anything about this creator's other qualities. I still don't take Torah literally or anything like that, and John tends to be appalled by my casual attitude toward scripture. I speculate about theology, and within what I believe there's a lot of flexibility as to God's nature. I don't talk about the experience usually--I told John and a few other people I knew would believe me. Most people would probably write it off as a hallucination, especially in rationalist-type circles, and I have no interest in debating it or proselytizing. Take it as you will. For my part, I'm pretty sure that God is real, and spoke to me directly.

2 things come to mind. While reading a book on Zen Buddhism, for a few moments, as I looked up, I felt as if I could see the structure underlying all reality in front of me, as if what we saw was paint upon a canvas.

Second, I once had a very vivid dream that I was killed in an accident. Due to method, there were a couple of seconds to see it coming. In that moment, in the dream, I didn't really feel afraid. It was a feeling of acceptance (I saw it coming and there was no way to avoid it). I thought something like "well, that's it then, there's nothing I can do" And a strong feeling of... letting go. It was as if every care and responsibility I ever had lifted from my shoulders, and I could feel it go. A sense of the world passing from my care into the care of everyone who would be left, like "none of this belongs to me anymore". It was a feeling of sublime peace and acceptance. It was the most deeply affecting dream I've ever had, and that sense of peace stayed with me for weeks afterwards.

ZOMG the following section just reminded me of something I learned when I was a kid and which felt really spooky at the time. This would be performed on a willing subject, who was asked to keep their arms closed (I never did this with a blindfold). They were asked to imagine that their arms were rising, while leaving them relaxed but not actually moving them. The practitioner would repeat a series of gestures (described below) a few times, then "pull" on non-existent ropes and at that time the subject's arms would start moving up; subjects would usually report not noticing this movement or performing it consciously, and were usually surprised when opening their eyes and seeing their arms raised and not hanging parallel to their bodies. The actions were light clapping twice on each side of the subject's head (a few inches away); snapping one's fingers at the same position, again twice for each side; then, without touching the arm, the performer of the "ritual" would move their hands as if braiding strands of rope around one of the subject's arms. It is after repeating this clapping-snapping-braiding a few times that the performer would pull on the "rope" and the corresponding arm would slowly come up. I think sometimes the direction of the arm coming up wasn't totally aligned with the direction of the pull, as in, pulling forwards but the arm rising sideways. The only explanation I have for this is suggestion, but it is a bit weird that the subject does not see which arm is being "pulled", or when.

column237:
Please disregard my answer for "Police Crime Rating" above, as this answer is more accurate regarding that.

On December 1, 2006 I was attending a demonstration against a rise in bus fares here in Sao Paulo. As it happened, I was pretty much in front of the mass of people (but not in a leadership role, it just so happened that I was walking faster than most people). I was taking pictures of police officers, who were not wearing name tags; at the time I believed they were mandated by law to do so and it was fundamentally illegitimate for them to use any amount of non-self-defensive force without their name tags, it's as if they were private citizens. Anyway, as the march was turning from a square into a big avenue I was insistently asking an officer about his absent name tag and he decided to arrest me.

He grabbed me, tearing my t-shirt; at this point what had been a peaceful interaction with protestors turned into tear gas and other kinds of crowd control being used, people running everywhere, chaos. I was dragged behind a closed newsstand and the officer who had grabbed me said something to the effect of "this is for the time one of you (protestors) hit me with a bottle", and hit me in the head with his baton. After what felt like quite a long time, I was taken to the police car to be taken to the station; inside the car, other officers were insistently asking me what I had done. I knew they had nothing on me and were trying to frame me, so I remained silent (we don't have anything like Miranda rights in Brazil). Part of these attempts to screw with me involved spraying pepper spray right on my face. I think at this point I was handcuffed, so I don't remember if I could at least follow my reflex of scratching my face. I was then taken to the precinct, fingerprinted, hit with a baton one more time (this time on my leg), and taken to a cell.

There was nobody else there and it was quite spacious, I was afraid it was gonna be horribly crowded and I was gonna have to interact with inmates. After a while, a lawyer for the organization calling the march came, talked to me and, after a couple more hours, got me released; the charge they were considering was something ridiculous like "obstruction of police work". I think it was at this very same day I said I wanted to get a forensic exam so the violence I'd suffered could be documented. When I saw a doctor working for the police department, he told me the examination could only be carried out if I stripped bare, even though I wasn't claiming to have suffered anything related to my private parts. Still I acquiesced, as I wanted to have evidence. But I don't think anything came of that exam; I later tried to file a complaint in the police department's inspector office (I'm not sure how to say this in English, they're the ones supposed to punish bad cops); however, even though I saw the cop who hit me in the head while I was walking downtown about a month after the incident, they were very uncooperative and said I could only proceed if I could identify the guy from a passport-sized photo, among a huge pile of papers, one for every cop that was in the area that day. I felt really bad about not being able to prosecute those sons of bitches; the whole system is totally rigged in their favor.

I also think I'd never told this, at least not with this level of detail, to anyone in the rat community.

column158:
The "ghost" experience: when I was around 8 or 9, I got up to go to the bathroom and saw a ball of light float out of the storage area in my brothers' room, which then came towards me. I turned and leapt down the stairs - the entire staircase for a two story house - which passed in slow motion. I landed on feet and hands, normal time resumed, and when I looked back up the light was gone. The crash was very loud however, and my parents were startled something fierce.

The ESP experience: I rarely but consistently experience deja reve, the feeling of having already dreamed an experience that is happening. The key detail is that mine sometimes give me predictive power: I have stepped out of the road and avoided a car I did not (consciously) know was coming; I have been able to redirect conversations to avoid argument; and one time I dreamt an actor was leaving a show which I did not follow, but we were able to confirm by searching for it specifically in Google. I have rarely been able to explicitly remember these dreams as dreams, before the situation they foresaw began. There is one that I had in November 2008 that I still half-expect to experience.

I experienced myself as my father and understood (in that moment) that I was his consciousness and that my consciousness would pass into my children if I had any, and that this meant that all consciousness is connected at the root of life and that we all share the one consciousness.

I tried some yoga poses in the shower and performed them expertly as I have never done before.

I experimented with sex, basically without touching anything got the hardest erection of my life by directly controlling the muscles and tissues necessary, and felt like I came without touching anything, but I don't think I actually did come and instead just pissed.

The whole experience lasted about 30 minutes, though it was hard to tell and it's hard to remember, then I felt sort of normal again.

column165: I had what I would call a "negative mystical experience" at age 12. It happened out of nowhere when I was sitting on my living room floor one evening. The experience involved all of the typical characteristics of mysticism (feeling of oneness with the universe, lack of sense of time / feeling of eternity, etc.), but it was profoundly "inverted," and I experienced it as horrifying. I experienced 2-3 months of depression / moderate derealization afterwards, for which I was taken to a psychiatrist and prescribed SSRI's. This may be some obvious psychotic experience that you should exclude if you recognize it as such, but I haven't had any other psychotic symptoms since then. The experience had a profound effect on my life, mood, and interest in philosophy/religion.

column158:
Had two disturbingly vivid and similar dreams being forcefully floated up by a flying saucer, through the roof of my house (which I remember was confusing during the dream how this was possible). The second dream was especially vivid, and I woke up right after, feeling unusually awake (in the room next to where I dreamed I was beamed up). To the point where I was slightly confused if it was an actual dream. Which had not happened before.

Both dreams were quite short. I remember sitting at my desk in my study room (which was next to my bedroom), looking outside, as a disc shaped craft approached, moving in a strange way (like a heavy leaf falling of a tree). I remember getting excited about seeing what looked like some otherworldly craft. It shortly after floated above my house where I could not see it (this was top floor of house). Then I remember becoming weightless, being pulled upwards. I remember I wanted to scream, but for some reason I could not, I also remember strong panic setting in, and a confused feeling how it was possible floating through the ceiling. Then I remember passing out (similarly how I passed when I was being sedated for surgery once when I was a teenager). And the dream ended.

The second one was extremely similar, except this time I did not get excited, but felt wary as the silvery disk approached. And the same thing repeated again, except this time it all felt more vivid and real, and I woke up right after feeling very awake. Thinking what the hell was that. Both dreams had no distortions or weirdness (besides the ufo and floating through the ceiling part).

A year or two after this the whole story of Fravor and the tic tacs broke (which was an extremely convincing ufo sighting in my opinion), and ever since my beliefs on possible alien visits have changed from not really on my radar, to plausible.

I semi-frequently get “meta deja-vu's”, i.e. while in random situations (usually conversations) i clearly remember having had a deja-vu-like “vision” some years in the past, a vision of this exact situation playing out, including any thoughts i am having during it (including, even, the meta-deja-vu, etc). 
If (and only if) i concentrate on this „post-premonition“ it becomes more and more convincing, as if my minds in these to points in time were in some way entangled and letting thoughts cross through in both directions, until it all dissolves in a puff of confusion.
I never remember any such premonitions before the corresponding situation happened, which puts a bit of a damper on this “ability” ...

My mother died of cancer 1 year after my birth. For the next 3 years (age 1-3) during workdays I was cared for by my aunt (fathers sister) and uncle. Their son, my cousin, is 11 yrs older. We don’t see each other very often but we are very close when we do. Doesn’t feel like a brother, but still close and personal. I still call my aunt „mum“ though. 
My father always took me home during weekends and when I was old enough I „came home“ permanently again. At the time I spent at my aunt’s, my older sister was „normally“ at home with my father, being cared for by my grandmother during the day if needed.

Ghost': I saw a humanoid figure in the middle of the road in my peripheral vision while I was driving home from work (in broad daylight on Halloween). It wasn't there when I checked my mirrors. It was distinct enough that I had to look over my shoulder to confirm. I am very confident that this does not require an appeal to the paranormal to explain, but it was weird enough that it was memorable.

'ESP': In my house we joke about the 'in-house psychic network' because of synchronicity; often I'll plan to suggest a restaurant for dinner all day, and my mother suggests it before I can; and my sisters say they were going to suggest it too. Sometimes I'll start to text someone in my family, only for them to text me first. I suspect this is just survivorship bias; only the coincidences are memorable, non-coincidences are forgotten.

column37:
Doing good with money is a hard problem; a lot of charities are ineffective or counterproductive. One effective solution is to keep your charity local, contributing to programs you can see the effects of and evaluate yourself; it probably won't be the best charity out there, but at least it cuts down on really bad-case scenarios, like accidentally funding brutal dictators. Effective Altruism is a movement of people who are evaluating high-value charities that I am not qualified to evaluate, and who seem to be trustworthy. That allows me to contribute to higher-value charities than I otherwise would, which in turn makes me inclined to contribute more. And SSC introduced me to EA (and still provides a good deal of my general information about it; I'm not actively involved in the EA community, I just appreciate their work.) 

(Also, while I checked no other boxes, I find knowing about predictive processing - and various other psychology essays over the years - useful in dealing with how my mind works. I haven't got a mental illness, but I still occasionally get predictive processing errors (ie: "someone is talking in a foreign language; I believe I recognize words; I'm wrong;" or "someone yells something close to my name, and I hear my name"), and knowing why is helpful. Also, knowing about biases is useful for avoiding procrastination and so on.

column37: After reading about Giving What We Can, I decided to donate 10% of my income to charity. I don't agree with the other part of the pledge about donating to do the most good, as I feel that leads to motivated reasoning: if you want to believe that AI risk is the "most good" because all your friends work on it and they're all very smart, you'll wind up finding convincing arguments even if they're not actually true (I particularly disagree with the arguments for existential risk that count potential humans that won't exist after extinction in the number of humans saved to multiply against the low chance of happening: I feel this argument encourages bribing people who wouldn't have children to pledge themselves and their descendants to have children, and it seems intuitively wrong that this could be a good use of charity money). I've also seen talk about the "most good" part allowing that people have different moral systems and can consider different things "good". I think as you go down this road you can get to any place you like, so it's better not to start on it in the first place. Instead, I've decided to give 10% of my income to whatever charities I feel like giving it to, which at the moment is a mix of ALLFED and the Internet Archive.

I don't know if this counts, but I'll include it because I think it is an experience that can be called "spiritual", if not in the traditional sense.

I have never formally studied astrophysics, but I am very interested in it. Once in a while I feel moved when I think about how boggling it is that we exist here on Earth with so many varied cultural and social norms that keep emerging and changing. Thinking about how much complexity and detail is at every zoom level of the universe, from quantum behavior to atoms to materials and physics interaction to bacteria and cells and tiny creatures to pets and humans and social expectations and clothing norms and signaling and friendship and love and the desire to create and earthquakes and atmospheric phenomena and planets in space and the ability to think about all of this. And then sometimes I feel like we're all in this together, the universe finding a way to observe itself.

Not on the same topic, but re: the energy stuff. Books like The Mind Body Prescription by Sarno influenced how I view recovery from injury in sports, and maybe chronic pain in people. I noticed on Hacker News there's always some posts in every thread about pain or injuries or sports or sedentary office worker problems (like carpal tunnel etc) that bring up how Sarno's book cured them. I have also had two times where I had pain (knee pain and then later, elbow pain) that strangely cleared up better after I used the principles in the book. So I think there's some weird stuff going on with the mind when it comes to healing or at least, feeling pain-free and confident in your body, and maybe that's why people believe in the reiki energy healing.

column37:
Not really a mental illness, I think - more that I have broad uncertainty and anxiety about the future and what I'm going to do.  I have marketable skills and my degree will probably be good enough to get an acceptably-paying job when I graduate, but I often fail to see the point, and I hate the idea of working on something inconsequential and actively degrading (like working a salaried job for a company to refine the dopamine-hack features of an app to compete with all the other addiction boxes in the marketplace, because it's what's incentivized).  I have a broad feeling along those lines that things are wrong, that huge amounts of talent are being wasted- spent on refining money-hunting programs to deploy in the zero-sum memetic ecosystem that siphons money and effort out of the economy and away from being used on the things that people would actually like it to be spent on.  I have no idea how accurate these intuitions are, but they cause me non-negligible stress when I think about my future employment.  Additionally, I feel like a fraud in my university (probably pretender complex, or whatever it's called; I don't go to the lectures I should on my course- I've done well enough in exams etc., but I can't muster up the will to go and sit in a crammed room for hours every day of the week, so I don't feel like a proper member of the physics community at my uni.) 

So, all that being said - good catharsis, btw, thanks - some of your posts have, in the past, given me an alternate point of view of things that put things into perspective and let me view some parts of my life, and some of the decisions I could make, as being a lot more potentially meaningful than my intuitions had implied before.  I'm mostly referring to I CAN RELATE TO EVERYONE EXCEPT THE OUTGROUP and MEDITATIONS ON MOLOCH.

Unsong was pretty fun, too.

column158:
I've had an experience of an apparently very direct empathy. Usually I have a very difficult time identifying with others' emotions due to autistic tendencies, although count myself as a kind, empathetic person. I just can't tell how others are feeling, or misinterpret things.

I was with a friend, who most likely had an undiagnosed personality disorder with narcissistic and antisocial tendencies. I remember looking up at him and suddenly experiencing an intense surge of feelings and reactions which I could not identify with. We kept looking each other in the eye for maybe half a minute, and throughout that time a very deep, chaotic yet somehow reasonable cluster of emotions such as anger, confusion, rage, sorrow, hatred and shame flowed through me like a current. Then it passed.

It wasn't that I cognitively thought that he looked angry or sad or whatever. It was that we looked at one another and I felt the current of experiences going through me, which I could not identify with, and I immediately interpreted them as his experiences. I felt a connection.

On our way out, I indirectly asked him about the moment, and he replied: "I don't know. I just felt very sad. Somehow I just felt very sad." He had a difficult time expressing his emotions in words other than 'happy', 'sad' or 'pissed' (alexithymia, I guess).

That has never happened afterwards or before. I do not suffer from psychotic illness or depression.

I have also occasionally had dreams and experiences which seem to reflect later events (precognition): I'm quite certain this is a feature of my brain's meaning-making machinery (that I intuitively interpret such connections and they seem to make sense to me). I would not say I believe these connections are real per se, but my mind produces such artifacts at times.

column165:
I had a period in my life where I experienced occasional derealization, perhaps due to anxiety. During that time I experienced a few intense moments where I did not feel anxious, but instead felt a deep, meaningful connection towards everything else - that is, I identified with everything that was going on. These experiences usually degraded into full-blown anxiety attacks. I can't say whether the intensity and alienness of the 'spiritual' moments caused the anxiety, or whether I was prone to anxiety attacks which were sometimes preceded by an intense spiritual experience. Anxiety wasn't always preceded by 'spiritual' experiences, but 'spiritual' experiences always lead to anxiety of varying levels.

(I was raised in a religious village, although my family was atheistic)

I recall once walking home, beginning to feel the interconnectedness again. I felt a "deep peace", a deep sense that everything is alright and that I am a part of something greater than myself; I was drawn towards that idea and felt my psychological boundaries dissolving with the greater whole. Then I thought: "Oh no, am I going to find religion now? Is this me going religious? No no no, I don't want it. Jesus, do not come into my heart. Stay away from my heart, Jesus, damnit, I don't want to believe in your love!" I went home and to sleep, lying in my bed, having a wonderful sense of belonging and connectedness and being scared shitless because of it. Then I fell asleep and felt normal again in the morning.

I also have had a few extremely intense hypnagogic spiritual experiences; once I "realized" that the birth of our universe is still happening, and that everything that is happening is the cosmic birth going on in a one, everlasting moment, that the world is being born over and over again instantaneously for ever and ever. The realization just occurred, I felt extremely exhilarated by it and then woke up feeling very disoriented and anxious. I fell asleep and everything was normal again in the morning, although I felt shaken up.

I do not suffer from psychotic illness, and these events only occurred in my twenties. I still have occasional attacks of mild hypomania, which then lead to anxiety. However, they are rare and the intensity of the experiences is such that I can control and manage them.

I was told to stop plying Morrowind (a video game) while we were praying for someone on a missions trip in mexico when i was 15. It was a still and small voice, but resolute. it was the voice of God.

The phrase was "Stop playing that game" and then a burst of imagery/feeling making it apparent it was about morrowind, and that i should stop

 I denied it 2 times, noting to myself internally "thats not what I we are praying about" and the same words and feeling came back. The words were with out question in my head. I took it hard, I really like that game I began to bargain (see context). Eventually I complied and I did not speak to anyone about this until much later in life (27ish?)

Context: I had been playing the game with an obsession over the previous few months, my final semester of my Sophomore year of HS suffered for it. I was spending 10 to 14 hours playing the game even ignoring sleep.

column158: When I was about 3 or 4 I thought I had telekinesis, but it turns out that I have some sort of weakness in my right eye such that I can move it independently of the left, causing double vision. Sometimes it seems that things and people have an "aura" about them (not visually, but ... synaesthetically?) Sometimes I either hear or forget that I thought about something, so that it seems like I was hearing music or heard someone say something such as my name. But I don't think any of these are actually "paranormal", I think it was my perception and that I pay attention to it and think about it more than other people do. Except that I once saw a UFO - this was different than the above because I actually stared at it for about 30s (as opposed to brief sounds or confusion about what I had perceived). It was a red glowing rod that traveled across the sky in daylight, slowly and into the clouds after which I could no longer see it. It made no sound and didn't appear like a plane.
column165: I have an extreme sense of connectedness when doing international folk dances. I have a similar but slightly different feeling sometimes when playing certain pieces of music in concerts, or when thinking about them or listening to them. I can't decide if it is less or more connected - either way it feels more "smooth" if that makes any sense - like I don't exist anymore and the world is only music is just flowing through me and everything. I have a more "disconnected" but as if I am separate from everything or like everything isn't really real sort of experience a lot - sometimes when walking alone, when I went to Iceland during the shortest days of the year, sometimes when walking outside at night. It sounds "dissociative", but it is a sort of peaceful but melancholic feeling. I have a religious experience despite not ever being religious. During certain pieces of music I feel God - when playing Vaughan Williams's Hodie in a concert (the most strong and I considered becoming religious after it), subsequently listening to recordings of the piece, and when listening to Janáček's Glagolitic Mass.

column165:
Occasionally when deep in a long session of very painful physical activity I feel that I mentally enter the presence of a kind of deity. It has an ambiguous, dark nature similar to Ares, both a potential bringer of victory and cruelty; the "deity" I encounter is a dualistic embodiment of mankind's potential for violence and of nature's (as in existence's) inherent absolute disregard for humanity's desire for the absence of suffering. It seems to speak with its own voice in a verbalization of universal laws; in the moments when I encounter it, it seems cynically disinclined to falsehoods, though it still has a perspective and dialogue, namely it mocks me for weakness (and acidly mocks more or less all of mankind for our palliative beliefs and aspirations for the cessation of violence and suffering). Where the ambiguity comes in is that it also indicates that what I'm doing is a sort of holy road to a higher state of being that has been forged in agony, where I am not thrown off whatever is my life path by pain, fear and uncertainty both due to being inured against those things through direct experience, and out of a self-preserving respect for the unstoppable and deadly movements of matter, energy and "history" in our reality.
I personally feel that this experience and experiences like it, including "divine" experiences of beatific mercy, connection, love and gratitude are inherent in human psychology on some level and this case serves a toughening purpose, but is rarely tapped into, perhaps never, depending on one's life arc, circumstances and inclinations. Psychedelic drugs may tap into these places without the normal prerequisites; while on LSD I experienced both that cold and alien reality of a universe that is not created bespoke for mankind, but also profound and humble love and appreciation for my friends and humanity's place in the universe.

column158:
ESP experience: I was playing a game of cards with 14 people, involving guessing the other person's move (out of two possible options), for about 1 hour. I got ~300 plays in the game correct. We calculated that the probability of this happening by chance was 1*10^ (some two digit number, I think around 90?). 

I don't believe in ESP, but I did *feel* like I was successfully reading people's faces to achieve this result. I could not replicate the experience in later games. I scored 33/36 the first time taking the Reading the Eyes in the Mind test. Between perceptiveness and luck I suppose everyone experiences at least one statistical "miracle" sometime.
column165:
1) I participated in stuff analogous to "energy work"/pranayama as part of normal hindu upbringing. After doing it, I experience temporarily greater control of attention and willpower, temporarily greater control over my physical reactions to emotional states, and temporarily elevated mood. No mystical effects, no effects lasting longer than 8 hours.

2) (Unrelated to the yoga above) I've experienced the loss of clear "I" boundary between myself and the rest of the universe as a result of thinking about consciousness really hard. It was a pretty thought. I started crying because it was overwhelmingly pretty.

The practical result is that I do not find the "hard problem of consciousness" and various related philosophy problems to be particularly confusing. The experience changed my stance on a few issues where these philosophical problems were confusing me (conceptions of soul dissolved, it became clearer that abortion was not bad, killing bacteria was not bad, probability that the universe might be animated by a god or other underlying consciousness reduced to near-zero, etc) - in other words, it made me less religiously inclined.

Sometimes, other people do find my deconstructions of these phenomenon compelling. On one occasion, I managed to explain this in a way that another person had the same experience. For the most part however life continues as normal.

column37:
Mental illness: maybe not SSC specifically, but the rationality community in general has helped me understand my own thinking better, and to show me that a lot of feelings and intuitions such as "I'm a terrible person" or "I will never amount to anything" etc. are just not based in reality. The EA community has also helped my mental health greatly by restoring a sense of purpose into my life, and both IRL communities I regularly attend (SSC/LW and EA) keep social isolation and loneliness at bay. 
Meat: I had been a vegetarian and then a pescatarian before I read SSC, and reverted back to omnivorism during an episode of depression. I might have gone back to vegetarianism again on my own anyways, but SSC/EA definitely had a role in encouraging me back to it. Also, in light of the recent AC on eating meat, I'm cutting eggs out of my diet and am currently re-evaluating whether I should eat fish. (I already eat clams and shellfish and stuff. )
I would for sure be donating to effective charities if I had an income, but I don't. 
AI safety career change: I wasn't sure if I should check the AI safety career change box, because I was strongly encouraged by SSC/LW to major in computer science instead of music, but it's technically not a career *change* as my career hadn't really started yet, and it also wasn't the only factor-- if I had gotten into my first choice music school it would have been a much harder choice, and I also had my parents pressuring me and future financial situation to think about. At the very least I can confidently say that SSC/EA is the reason that I feel great about my career path, instead of, like, forever regretting that I didn't go into music and hating myself for selling out and spiraling into depression and cynicism.

column165:
When I was 15 I thought I felt the presence of God very suddenly and powerfully. I was extremely depressed at the time. I remember staring out the window at a tree after having just had a conversation with a very close Christian friend, who I happened to have a crush on. I don't remember if that particular conversation was even about religion, but over the past month or so we had talked about religion a lot. So I was just looking at this tree and suddenly, I just got this feeling that God was all around me and I understood everything now and everything was charged with meaning and beauty. It seemed so clear and so obvious that He was just there the whole time, and that I had been blind to it my whole life. The feeling persisted powerfully for a few days or so (I remember checking every once in a while, almost in disbelief, as if to affirmed to myself "yep, it's still there"), and faded away over maybe a couple weeks. I was not religious before that, and I converted to Christianity almost immediately after. At the time, I was sure that God had healed my depression, and indeed I was very happy for maybe 4 months afterwards, but then fell back into depression. Nevertheless, I clung to my belief in God for another year and a half ish, and by the time I was introduced to the Lesswrong community after another half year it had waned completely.

Other than that one notable instance, I frequently feel spiritual connectedness, profundity, and overwhelming emotion while playing or listening to music, though I'm not sure if that counts. (How similar do you consider music to drugs?) I also often feel deeply peaceful and connected to nature while taking walks.

column158:
RE: ESP, I'm a strong skeptic on the phenomenon, but have had several low-probability, spooky-ish experiences with it. 

For one example, on a lark I wrote a binary guessing script (ie, enter a guess of 0 or 1, then report whether it matched the output of a prng) and tried to predict/affect the outcome with n=100. I would close my eyes, wait for whatever random noise process in my brain would make either 0 or 1 "feel right", then focus heavily on it while inputing my answer. I ended up getting in the low 60s correct, which is pretty unlikely though still well within the range of possibility, but at the time I was doing this, a large alocasia plant behind me had one of its stalks collapse. This is a regular event during the lifecycle of the leaves, but doesn't happen more than, say, once every few months, so it felt pretty weird at the time.

Another time, while sitting around engaged in unrelated business, a phrase occurred to me, the idea of a person having a "mind like a search engine", being a more temporally appropriate version of the phrase "mind like a steel trap". I used, of course, a search engine to see if I'd come up with a novel phrase, and didn't get any good hits, most being of the "[...] mind. Like a search engine, [...]" form. (More hits have materialized since this experience) I squirreled the phrase away for some later use, and went about my business. Perhaps a few days later, I decided to start reading a book I'd received as a gift (Oryx & Crake), for no particular reason, and partway through the book, discovered the exact phrase sitting there. At the time, this felt like some kind of reverse chronology, that I should have read the book first, and then looked up the phrase.

A final experience, which has the fun quality of having directly calculable probability came while playing a card game called Bang!, which is sort of like the game Mafia, played with cards that grant powers, etc. All the cards have text about their powers, ie you can use Bullet cards to shoot your opponents, but also have a regular poker suite as well. One card, called Peyote, allows you draw a card, and then if you can predict the color of the next card (ie red or black), you can draw another card. The EV, of course, is two cards (the same number you draw normally), but with some fun variance. A friend played this card, and guessed his first draw correctly, then his second, and then his third... and continued guessing correctly for 13 total cards. Everyone was kind of freaked out. The probability was 1 in 8192, so not exactly winning the lottery, but still spooky.

column158: When I was in high school, I had a dream where I woke up, ate breakfast, got on the school bus, and went to school, all in real time. I sat through my first period, listened to the professor... then woke up. I then got up, ate breakfast, got on the school bus, went to school... and it was all exactly the same as it was in my dream. The eeriest part about it was that I could actually anticipate what the teacher was saying and was saying the lecture under my breath a short bit ahead of the teacher, word for word. I'm not sure what the cause of this was; was it a weird case of deja vu? Simply recognizing patterns, the "strings that control the system" as it were, seeing how predictable things were? Was I truly recalling my dream accurately, or simply projecting things from the real world back into the dream? It was a very strange experience and I still have no real explanation, though I doubt it was anything supernatural.

For Spiritual. I have for years been haphazardly experiencing what I call the body of light, where if I focus on my lower back I can excite a feeling of energy up through my spine and to every single part of my body. It feels like a lovely electricity, and my muscles go all tense when it happens and my breathing and heart rate increase. column158:
I once encountered what I thought was an evil spirit or demon. I felt terrified and oppressed by what seemed like a supernatural evil force. I followed the teaching of my religion and commanded the demon to depart, in the name of Jesus Christ. I immediately began to feel lighter and and my fear subsided. 

I have also experienced sleep paralysis; I felt that an evil force of some sort was preventing me from moving. I recognized it as sleep paralysis, so I knew the scientific explanation, but still prayed to ask Jesus Christ for help (mentally; I couldn't speak.) Gradually I was able to move again; I guess it was typical sleep paralysis. But still; I am not sure personally, since the sense of "evil" was very strong and relief came when I followed the teachings of my faith. 

Apologies if this crosses over into mystical experiences! Demons seem like they could go both ways.
column165:
I have had rare experiences where I felt clearly that I was talking with God. One specific example was when I was very depressed, and I wrote out questions about things that were bothering me. I wrote the replies, but it would be more accurate to say that I dictated the responses, from God, as they came into my mind. I felt, and still feel, that this was God speaking to me. I did not hear a voice, but the words that came into my head weren't mine, and the sense of love and benevolence is still strong (this event was 23 years ago.)

I've experienced very unlikely things that could be considered miracles, but I've also had cases where I WANTED a miracle and didn't see one, so while I expect it's possible, I am very careful to say whether a thing is a miracle or not.

column158:
There are a couple so it would take a while to describe them all, but the one that stands out the strongest is:
I was driving with a friend in the car in my early twenties, and I started to feel a sensation of an intense wind blowing my whole body, but we were in the car with the windows closed. The feeling increased, and I started to hear a rushing sound that got louder and louder. 

I pulled the car over and said something to my friend that I had to stop and take a breather, I got out of the vehicle, and the world went white, my body and field of vision were gone. In that space, there was a sense of unity, and something like voices started to speak, and there with me wisdom about life and being incarnate.
They were inside me and Outside me at At the same time, gradually They showed Me this Glowing light That each Life is Born with, And the Experiences that We pick Up that occlude this light. These were the pains that separate us from ourselves, something like that. That to be an Angel/ a bodhisattva was to be born knowing what would happen to you. And yet to come anyway.
This whole thing had the sense of many presences communicating with me but not actually ”talking” to me.
 As the lesson from this presence was concluding I could still see the this glowing light from inside people and the normal world faded back into view.

I don't know how to classify the experience but it felt more real than most waking experiences and wasn't from any drugs or anything else I could point my finger to.

column165:
Spiritual: I sometimes have ecstatic experiences.  It feels like a combination of being deeply moved, as by a beautiful story, song, or artwork, along with extreme joy, and sometimes (only in the strongest cases) chills or shivers, that comes suddenly.  No external prompt is needed.  It most often happens when I think about something awe-inspiring and good, whether true or fictional (but only things associated with people or persons--so thinking about God's goodness or a particularly heroic act might do it, but contemplating the vastness of the universe has never worked), though I have also had it happen when thinking about nothing in particular while admiring beautiful nature, textbook shopping, or riding a bike.  It feels profoundly important.  While in this state, I feel overflowing goodwill for everyone/thing I meet, and others' happiness makes me happy as if it were my own.

Religious: I've had the above experience while praying and some (but not all) of them felt particularly like being in the presence of God.  However, it did not feel like "contact" with any particular entity, in the same way that being submerged in the sea doesn't feel like carrying water in a water-tight bag.

When looking at a *really* shaggy rug, sometimes the areas outside of foveal vision look like they're wriggling or writhing in a barely perceptable way, but only if I focus intensely on one spot for like 20 seconds or more.

column165:
When I was 19 I climbed a mountain in Mexico (I’m American) and then climbed on top of a very old pyramid/temple at the top. Up there, I met God. It was an elaborate experience, but it was like being accosted by the feelings of hundreds of thousands of people all at once and understanding for the first time that I had never been alone through any of my suffering and that God was with me every step of the way if only I had reached for Him. It felt like a tactile experience but also the words/communication were all mind to mind. There was no visual. 

I also used to get visited by the Virgin Mary in my bed after I was sexually molested as a child, to comfort me. As an adult I’m fairly certain that was a hallucination I made up in order to feel safe and loved in an environment in which I felt neither.

column165:
Not sure if it counts, but I had an episode of depersonalisation (I'd never heard of the term beforehand, but I looked it up afterwards and the descriptions I read rang very true) a few years ago. Just before I went to bed I was looking in the mirror, and it came on suddenly. I can't think of anything in particular that could have triggered it, and this is the only time I've felt this in my life.

It's hard to put into words exactly how it felt, but I suddenly couldn't figure out why "I" (the thing doing the thinking) cared so much about the person I saw in the mirror. Why is that person in particular so important that I spend so much time worrying about all the little details of their life? Not an in intellectual sense, I legitimately had no idea. The two concepts of "self" (the thing doing the thinking vs the person with my name, standing in that room) were completely detached from each other.

This puzzled but calm state only lasted for a few seconds before I realised that something was wrong. While the two "self"s were still separate, I could tell that something was wrong. That I shouldn't feel that way, even if I couldn't figure out why, or what I should be feeling instead. It was a *very* intense feeling, and I quickly became quite terrified, like I was adrift in some way. It's probably the most scared I've ever been in my life.

I wandered around in a bit of a daze, which felt very strange, like it wasn't "me" walking around, but I was just remote controlling someones body. This only lasted about 10 seconds before I suddenly snapped back into myself and felt normal again. Once this happened I was still quite on edge, and it took me several minutes to calm down again.

I don't attribute any spiritual or religious significance to this event - just something bizarre happening in my brain.

column158: I've encountered many ghosts, hallucinations, telepathy-like experiences, "banshees", aliens etc etc. As a child I often saw Grey Aliens outside of my window, when my father died I heard a "banshee" scream (something he believed in strongly, he believed in much New Age and irish mythology type stuff), I have constant visual hallucinations (mostly LSD-like fractal patters, much more elaborate than usual Phosphenes), I often have "premonitions" to not trust people that turn out to be true sometimes only a long time in the future. All these experiences have reasonable explanations that do not require invoking the supernatural. For a few years I was highly psychotic/schizoid (during this time I had much more intense experiences such as being "mind controlled" by aliens, talking to god, etc), but this turned out to be a treatable sugar disorder (Metformin completely normalized any unpleasant symptoms). I have been evaluated as very psychologically stable, but still experience frequent phenomena that could be interpreted as supernatural, but are also easily explainable as mild neurological quirks. They do not inhibit my life, if anything they are good "rationality training".

Inspired by "The Control Group is Out of Control," I decided to conduct a parapsychology study for a school project that basically had us doing an experiment. I tested whether I could control people's minds. I got a tally counter, then had people click it for 30 seconds while I was hiding out of sight, either doing nothing or thinking "push the button" at them. While I do not believe in ESP or the like, I certainly was hoping to get an interesting result.

Which I did indeed. With a decent sample size, the folks in the control group clicked the tally counter substantially more than the people in the treatment group. I designed the experiment as well as I could (and, in an absolute sense, I think as well as most actual psychology experiments), so this was a disquieting and entertaining result. I strongly suspect my results were just a coincidence (or possibly stemming from some unknown flaw in my experimental design), but as a proper Bayesian, I do have to update in favor of ESP being a thing.

column165: I used to be religious; was raised mildly Catholic but became more serious about it as a teenager. During worship or orayer I felt several times where it seemed like I had a sense of a presence. Usually this was a fuzzy sense of personhood associated with a positive emotion such as love, caring, reassurance or awe/majesty. Very occasionally this was associated with an idea, message, or prompt to action. Occasionally this was paired with a few words or short sentence. At the time this fit into the framework of my religion, but now I believe that it was 70% in my head to 30% the emotion of a shared worship setting or quiet contemplation, and don't ascribe any supernatural significance or cause to it. Now that I do not practise religion, I have no mystical experiences.

column37:
I have most benefited from your approach and way of thinking about things.  The LW arguments are not soldiers type of thinking has been important along with your detailed analysis of journal articles and the nature of studies.  I work at a University and have done hard science pharmaceutical research with a few publications and now work in educational support on the soft sciences side with a few publications and conferences from that.  

Your approaches which vary from hard to soft skepticism have greatly improved my own thinking and approach to research and work.  I have also started giving to charities more recently after your work on effective altruism and very seriously considering for the first time why I did or did not give to charities.  I found I had no reason not to and have also changed my investments for retirement and banking habits to support altruistic causes and environmentally sounds approaches.  I am considering changing my career as well to be aligned with my values.

Most of all you've demonstrated to me the world is not entirely filled with morons and that there are intelligent people out there whom I can respect - who also suffer from the same sort of isolation and pain I've experienced being surrounded by folks who do not get it.

column158:
Was into occult, martial arts, and Transcendental Meditation when in high school. Was trying to explore/investigate/develop occult/paranormal powers. Mostly it came down to playing mind games with/on friends or other students and teachers. In retrospect, was using some rational dark arts and mindfulness practice to influence my own and their perceptions. I really wanted it to be real but kept running into disconfirming evidence.
Then I got "saved" by some charismatic (Columbus Oh Home Church ca 1976 ) christians. Had some experiences that I interpreted as "channeled demons vs Jesus" events. 
Then I tried to be a good christian and make it work. Read the bible through 5 times, memorized passages, active in church and community outreach, fervent in prayer. But again, kept running into disconfirming evidence. The best way to make an atheist is have a religious person really read their book, take it literally and seek internally consistency.
When I became post-christian, I briefly investigated other beliefs looking for the one true way. But they all seemed to sell the same bronze-age mind-games. I looked briefly at wicca, and found it was generally about willing self-deception, which I wasn't willing to do. 
In my late 20s I became a rational skeptic. Then Internet, cell phones, and math = firm atheist.
About 10 years ago, my son introduced me to Less Wrong. Wow! It took me years to get through the sequences, and I know it's not all settled science and subject to becoming more right, but the drop on cognitive dissonance is amazing. Now I feel I'm on the path to the Way.

I closed my eyes and saw a blue luminous worm crawling from the darkness, directly toward my eyes. It made a deep bass sound that steadily grew louder. I opened my eyes and didn't see or hear the worm. I checked the time on my alarm clock.

I closed my eyes again, and the worm had gotten closer, as though it had continued crawling towards my eyes while they were open.

When the worm reached my eyes, it blossomed into a glowing white lattice of runes and I heard something like a chorus of angels. They were beautiful, but not human and not speaking words. Just singing.

The lattice and chorus faded. My closed eyes saw darkness again. I opened them, checked the time. Only a minute had passed.

I have never had such an experience before or since. It came at the culmination of a year of trauma therapy, confronting my deepest fears for 3 days straight, and finally conquering them.

column158:
I often assume the existence of harmful entities in places I can't obtain information on (dark corners, unexplored alleys, etc) even if I know they are places were it people can't be (e.g. the room I just left and turned the light of off; a road corner that is only accessible by the exit I'm currently taken, and I was just there; etc). My mind will often go "but there can be someone there NOW you CAN'T know for SURE" even though the event has ~0% probability.
Also one specific case from when I was a child, where I played a game of "every time a train is crossing the railroad I have to hide or The Big Bad Wolf will get me", and that even now influences me, even though it was a game created by me, I feel an overwhelming urge to hide from trains in my hometown (but nowhere else), and if I don't I get the feeling that something is Very Deeply Wrong and I MUST hide (I can usually fight this instinct, but when there's a quick & easy hiding place, I still fall prey to it)

column165: It is somewhat normal to feel feelings close to "an extreme sense of connectedness, profundity, or presence that seemed completely distinct from ordinary life", which I usually obtain when acquiring knowledge about subjects I knew a bit before, but which are now being deepened. It never happened when I was purposefully studying a certain subject, but it does happen when I'm acquiring "accidental knowledge" (watching a documentary because I'm bored, reading wikipedia in "let's open all the tabs" mode, casually reading SSC). I've even started copy-noting the texts that trigger it when I can to see if I can find anything in common to them, and so far it seems mostly connected to discovery or confirmations of the human condition. Now that I think better of it, the feeling can more aptly be described as "this is true, and I believe it wholeheartedly" whereas with most knowledge there's always an associated probability estimate (and in hindsight, this also applies for these cases AFTER the fact; but during them there is full certainty that my world views are being validated, and are right, and are true)

column158:
One of my mothers is a practicing Pagan, so she taught me some fundamentals of magic when I was young (mostly meditative techniques, and what - in hindsight - were lessons on how to identify and get out of bad relationships). I still practice meditation.

Sometimes, when my mother or I feel unreasonably down, we will lend each other some of our energy. I've never observed this to break any physical laws, but it always makes the person receiving the boost feel better, and act more collected/less weepy/more energetic. I firmly believe that any effect this has is psychosomatic, and more likely based on A) being a literal show of support and care or B) on the placebo effect.

column165:
I would call my experience with magic (detailed above) to include energy work.

I also heard the following account directly from someone that I trust implicitly: when this person was accompanying another person to a chiropractic appointment that involved acupuncture, the chiropractor invited them to hold their hand over the needles, and they reported that the air above some of the needles was noticeably warmer than above other needles, with no other apparent cause.

That account leads me to believe that ideas of energy flow in the human body are related to _something_ (blood? exothermic chemical reactions?) which is not yet properly understood.

Finally, when I was a small child, I was afraid (in a serious, panic-and-flail limbs way) of the dark. (Or rather, any dark that was lower than my sleeping place. Dark sky? No problem) One night, I fell asleep downstairs while people were still in the house and the lights were still on. I woke up suddenly, after everyone had gone to bed, to the dark house. But rather than be scared, everything seemed still, calm, and peaceful. I just sat there in the dark (I don't know how long I was awake), and after that I had completely lost my fear of the dark. It was a deeply touching experience.

column165: When I was Catholic as a teen I went on a retreat, during which I “encountered God” in a deeply profound and intense way—I felt his presence, like he was wrapping his arms around me and wiping my tears away, and he cured me from specific PTSD symptoms and trauma from losing a loved one. Before that retreat for the past six months I had been crying myself to sleep every night, making plans to run away from home, becoming interested in crime, and generally drowning in grief and struggling to find anything of value in life, after having lost someone so close to me. After coming home from the retreat, I never cried for the lost person again, and I didn’t grieve. I walked away from that moment with God having been fundamentally changed. The effect lasted for years (maybe forever, it’s hard to tell since of course I continued to change as I entered adulthood) and my friends said I was like a different person afterwards. To this day, when I think of the lost person I don’t feel sad, but I feel a warm sense that God has blessed me with the memory of her (though I think the feeling can be explained purely naturalistically).

column158:
Sometimes I get what seems to be precognition. While sleeping/almost dreaming, my mind will wander into making up scenarios that then actually later happen to a completely unreasonable and unknowable level of detail. I'm talking specific sensations on the level of the light on the pattern of wallpaper in the background of the room, and the colour of the carpet/bed unfocused in the background, plus the tactile anticipation of exactly how someone would be touching me, plus many many other 'inside-perspective' sensory details of one specific moment, months or even years in advance. This leads to deja vu so strong it can be nearly debilitating. 

It's never useful or helpful or anything. I just sometimes anticipate the entire detailed sensorium of moments in my life, half a year or more in advance, while half-asleep. The moments usually aren't significant, but most of the examples which I've noticed and remembered/selected as "holy shit this is a thing" were indeed around distinctive/unexpected events -- kissing one boyfriend while sitting in his lap in his room (and then I had to call off the makeout session in surprise/shock, at least for a bit), playing this one specific mobile game on my tablet while at a hacker con in an interesting building interior (and then I lost focus on the talk because goddam and mentioned it to my girlfriend later). 

Yes, I'm certain on the causality -- that first I predict, and then I notice that moment happening. Yes, the level of detail is completely unreasonable for regular speculation, and includes things I absolutely had no way to know or predict in advance. It's always very much in first person and multisensory, usually with a focus on touch-texture and colour/shape/space and bodyposition and concious-understanding/mental-task. No, I don't have a written or mental list of 'upcoming' possible things -- I would like to have this, though. I'm not sure if I can pick out the sensation at the time of something predictive vs just dreaming while half asleep, so I tried keeping a dream diary for it, but ran into general executive function issues when trying to start the habit of using it consistently. Plus, it's pretty rare, and I don't even know if that sense of predictive-dreaming vs just dreaming is real, and if it is then the qualia of it is subtle and indescribable. 

I wouldn't call it premonitions. I would say it feels magical in a weird, intense, disturbing way that makes me question reality. If it was frequent and direct-able, it'd be a superpower, but as is I just get too much deja vu, if there's anything going on at all. 

I've mentioned it to others maybe 3 times, for people I trust hugely. One mentioned that she gets dreams of people before bad things happen to them, and it passes through her family. A year later she had a dream of me, called me while distressed, then nothing especially bad happened.  Neither of the others had anything similar going on.

At one point I went to a christian event that ended being a big preaching/motivational/concert/stuntshow thing, and got *way* too into it. I absolutely got talked into a sense of connectedness and purpose that was striking at the time. 

Afterwards, noticing that the rest of my youth group wasn't nearly as into it and in fact seemed vaguely embarrassed by my behavour was like a bucket of cold water to the face - shocking and disillusioning. Later I stopped 'questioning' and left the church entirely. But for a moment there, I was very much a true believer.

column173: I have an annoying number of floaters due to age and severe myopia. Also, what seems to be neurological vision weirdness that my eye doctors can't really pin down: the static I see is EXTREMELY comparable to raw CCD noise or looking at the graininess of laser light. Most people's brains denoise their vision, but I perceive (as far as the doctors can surmise) the individually excited rods and cones. I literally did not know other people did not share my experience this until last year when trying to follow up on vision changes that are likely just age and severe myopia related, and I had to explain what I had always seen to three different people who were kind of flabbergasted at what I was describing. I can ALWAYS notice my vision artifacts when I focus on them, but since it's "normal" to me, it's not usually intrusive unless I'm looking at a uniform surface (like a computer screen with a light background, or cloudless skies). I also get a weird halo afterimage if I stare at something with extreme contrast, like an eye chart, worse if I have one eye closed. I assume this one is because my prescription is so strong I see chromatic aberration changes depending on where I look through the lens, and I assume my brain is working overtime to figure that shit out, more so whenever I take my glasses off.

So I spun out of the freezer to flee, and totally did not brush against the singing magnet on the fridge that then started singing. (I blame infrasound and anxiety.
